passages.title: The Muses dance on Helicon
passages.summary: The Muses wash in sacred waters and dance on Mount Helicon.

verses.text: Let us begin our song with the Muses of Helicon,
who live on Helicon, the great and sacred mountain,
and on soft feet, around the violet-dark spring
and the altar of mighty Zeus, son of Cronus, they dance.
After washing their tender skin in the waters of Permessus,
or the Horse’s Spring, or the sacred river Olmeius,
they form their dances on the highest slopes of Helicon,
beautiful, lovely dances, their feet moving with vigor.

notes.label: Muses
notes.general: Goddesses who inspire song and poetry.
notes.here: They dance on their sacred mountain.

notes.label: Helicon
notes.general: A mountain in Greece associated with the Muses.
notes.here: Its springs and heights are places where they wash and dance.

notes.label: Zeus
notes.general: The ruler of the Greek gods.
notes.here: The Muses dance around his altar.

notes.label: Cronus
notes.general: A god of the older generation, called the Titans.
notes.here: He is named as Zeus’s father.

notes.label: Altar
notes.general: A structure where people make offerings to a god.
notes.here: This altar belongs to Zeus.

notes.label: Permessus
notes.general: A river near Mount Helicon.
notes.here: One of the waters where the Muses bathe.

notes.label: Horse’s Spring
notes.general: A spring on Helicon, also called Hippocrene.
notes.here: Another bathing place for the Muses.

notes.label: Olmeius
notes.general: A river near Mount Helicon.
notes.here: Hesiod calls its waters sacred.

passages.title: The gods in the Muses' song
passages.summary: Hidden in mist, the Muses travel at night and sing about the gods.

verses.text: From there the Muses set out, wrapped in thick mist,
walking through the night, their beautiful voices rising,
singing of Zeus, who bears the aegis shield, and majestic Hera
of Argos, who walks in golden sandals;
of bright-eyed Athena, daughter of Zeus who bears the aegis;
of shining Apollo and Artemis, who showers arrows;
of Poseidon, who holds the earth and shakes it;
of honored Themis and Aphrodite with her curling lashes;
of Hebe crowned in gold and beautiful Dione;
of Leto and Iapetus, and Cronus with his crooked schemes;
of Eos the Dawn, great Helios the Sun, and bright Selene the Moon;
of Gaia the Earth, great Oceanus, and black Night;
and of the sacred family of all the other gods who live forever.

notes.label: Zeus
notes.general: The ruler of the gods and father of Athena.
notes.here: He carries the aegis and begins the list of gods.

notes.label: Aegis
notes.general: A divine protective object, pictured as a shield or cloak.
notes.here: Carrying it marks Zeus’s power.

notes.label: Hera
notes.general: Zeus’s wife and queen of the gods.
notes.here: She is linked with Argos and wears golden sandals.

notes.label: Argos
notes.general: A Greek city and surrounding region where Hera was worshipped.
notes.here: Hesiod calls Hera “of Argos.”

notes.label: Athena
notes.general: Zeus’s daughter, a goddess of wisdom, crafts, and warfare.
notes.here: She is described as bright-eyed.

notes.label: Apollo
notes.general: A god associated with music, prophecy, and archery.
notes.here: He is called shining, translating the name Phoebus.

notes.label: Artemis
notes.general: A goddess of hunting and Apollo’s sister.
notes.here: She showers arrows.

notes.label: Poseidon
notes.general: A god of the sea and earthquakes.
notes.here: He holds the earth and shakes it.

notes.label: Themis
notes.general: A goddess of justice and rightful order.
notes.here: The Muses sing of her with honor.

notes.label: Aphrodite
notes.general: The goddess of love and desire.
notes.here: Hesiod draws attention to her eyes or lashes.

notes.label: Hebe
notes.general: The goddess of youth.
notes.here: She wears a golden crown.

notes.label: Dione
notes.general: A goddess whose name is closely related to Zeus’s.
notes.here: She is praised as beautiful.

notes.label: Leto
notes.general: The mother of Apollo and Artemis.
notes.here: She is among the gods praised in the song.

notes.label: Iapetus
notes.general: One of the Titans, the older generation of gods.
notes.here: He appears alongside Leto and Cronus.

notes.label: Cronus
notes.general: A Titan and Zeus’s father.
notes.here: He is described as crafty in his planning.

notes.label: Eos
notes.general: Dawn imagined as a goddess.
notes.here: She is named alongside the Sun and Moon.

notes.label: Helios
notes.general: The Sun imagined as a god.
notes.here: Hesiod calls him great.

notes.label: Selene
notes.general: The Moon imagined as a goddess.
notes.here: She is described as bright.

notes.label: Gaia
notes.general: The Earth imagined as a goddess.
notes.here: She is included among the eternal gods.

notes.label: Oceanus
notes.general: The divine river believed to flow around the world.
notes.here: He is praised as great.

notes.label: Night
notes.general: Night imagined as a goddess, called Nyx in Greek.
notes.here: She is described as black.

notes.label: Immortal
notes.general: Able to live forever.
notes.here: The song praises the whole family of everlasting gods.

passages.title: The Muses call Hesiod to sing
passages.summary: The Muses speak sharply to Hesiod, then give him a staff and the power to sing about the gods.

verses.text: These Muses once taught Hesiod beautiful song
as he tended lambs below sacred Helicon.
These were the first words the goddesses spoke to me,
the Muses of Olympus, daughters of Zeus who bears the aegis:
“Shepherds who live in the fields, shameful creatures, nothing but bellies!
We know how to tell many lies that sound like the truth;
we also know, when we choose, how to speak the truth.”
So spoke great Zeus’s daughters, sure and skillful with words.
They gave me a staff, a branch of flourishing laurel
they had plucked, a wondrous sight, and breathed into me a voice
divine, so I could sing of things to come and things long past.
They told me to praise the family of blessed gods who live forever,
and always to sing of the Muses themselves, first and last.

notes.label: Hesiod
notes.general: The Greek poet speaking in this poem.
notes.here: He says the Muses taught him while he was tending lambs.

notes.label: Muses
notes.general: Goddesses who inspire poetry and song.
notes.here: They give Hesiod his poetic voice and tell him what to sing.

notes.label: Helicon
notes.general: A sacred mountain in Greece.
notes.here: Hesiod meets the Muses below it.

notes.label: Olympus
notes.general: The mountain home of the gods.
notes.here: Calling the Muses “of Olympus” connects them with the divine household.

notes.label: Zeus
notes.general: The ruler of the gods.
notes.here: He is the Muses’ father and carries the divine aegis.

notes.label: Nothing but bellies
notes.general: An insult suggesting that someone cares only about food.
notes.here: The Muses use it to mock the shepherds.

notes.label: Laurel staff
notes.general: A long stick made from a laurel tree, which has glossy evergreen leaves.
notes.here: The Muses give it to Hesiod as a sign of his new authority as a singer.

notes.label: Divine
notes.general: Coming from or belonging to the gods.
notes.here: Hesiod’s new singing voice comes from the Muses.

passages.title: What the Muses sing
passages.summary: The Muses fill Olympus with song about the gods’ beginnings, Zeus’s power, humans, and Giants.

verses.text: But why all this talk of oak or rock?
Come, let us begin with the Muses, who sing to their father Zeus
and delight his mighty mind within Olympus,
telling of what is, what will be, and what was before,
their voices joining as one. Their tireless song flows
sweetly from their mouths, and their father’s halls laugh,
the halls of thundering Zeus, as the goddesses’ lily-like voices
spread. The peak of snowy Olympus echoes,
and so do the homes of the immortal gods. Raising their deathless voices,
the Muses first praise in song the honored family of gods
from the beginning, those born to Gaia the Earth and wide Uranus the Sky,
and the gods descended from them, the givers of good things.
Next they sing of Zeus, father of gods and humans,
both as they begin their song and as they bring it to an end,
telling how far he surpasses the gods, how greatest he is in power.
Then, singing of the human race and the mighty Giants,
they delight Zeus’s mind within Olympus,
the Muses of Olympus, daughters of Zeus who bears the aegis.

notes.label: Oak or rock
notes.general: An old expression whose exact meaning here is uncertain.
notes.here: Hesiod uses it as he breaks off his personal story and returns to the Muses.

notes.label: Muses
notes.general: Goddesses of song and poetry.
notes.here: Their united voices delight Zeus and make Olympus echo.

notes.label: Olympus
notes.general: The mountain home of the gods.
notes.here: Its snowy peak and divine halls ring with the Muses’ song.

notes.label: Zeus
notes.general: The ruler of the gods and the Muses’ father.
notes.here: Their song celebrates his supreme power.

notes.label: Lily-delicate
notes.general: A comparison with a lily flower, suggesting delicacy and beauty.
notes.here: Hesiod uses the flower image to describe the goddesses’ voices.

notes.label: Gaia
notes.general: The Earth imagined as a goddess.
notes.here: She and Uranus are parents of an early generation of gods.

notes.label: Uranus
notes.general: The Sky imagined as a god.
notes.here: With Gaia, he fathers the gods whose family history the Muses sing.

notes.label: Giants
notes.general: A race of powerful beings in Greek myth.
notes.here: They are a separate subject of the Muses’ song, alongside humankind.

notes.label: Aegis
notes.general: A divine shield or protective cloak.
notes.here: It identifies Zeus as the powerful father of the Muses.

passages.title: How the Muses were born
passages.summary: Mnemosyne and Zeus have nine daughters, the Muses. Their songs help people forget their troubles.

verses.text: In Pieria, Mnemosyne lay with father Zeus, son of Cronus, and bore him the Muses,
she who rules the hills of Eleuther,
daughters who bring forgetfulness of troubles and relief from cares.
For nine nights wise Zeus lay with her,
climbing into her sacred bed, far from the other immortal gods.
When a year had passed and the seasons had turned,
as the months waned and many days ran their course,
Mnemosyne bore nine daughters, all of one mind, whose hearts
are set on song, their spirits free from care,
a little way from the highest peak of snowy Olympus.

notes.label: Muses
notes.general: Nine goddesses of song and poetry.
notes.here: Daughters of Zeus and Mnemosyne who bring relief from worries.

notes.label: Mnemosyne
notes.general: The goddess of memory. Her name means “Memory.”
notes.here: The mother of the nine Muses.

notes.label: Zeus
notes.general: King of the gods.
notes.here: The wise father of the Muses.

notes.label: Cronus
notes.general: Zeus’s father, who ruled the gods before him.
notes.here: The Greek calls Zeus “son of Cronus.”

notes.label: Pieria
notes.general: A region near Mount Olympus in northern Greece.
notes.here: Where Mnemosyne gives birth to the Muses.

notes.label: Eleuther
notes.general: An obscure place-name.
notes.here: Mnemosyne rules its hills.

notes.label: Olympus
notes.general: A mountain in Greece and the home of the gods.
notes.here: The Muses are born near its snowy summit.

passages.title: The Muses on Olympus
passages.summary: The nine Muses sing about the gods and their father Zeus as they go to Olympus.

verses.text: There the Muses have shining dancing grounds and beautiful homes.
Beside them the Graces and Himeros, Desire, have their homes
amid celebrations. Sending lovely voices from their mouths,
the Muses sing of the laws and praise the noble ways
of all the immortal gods, sending out their lovely voices.
Then the Muses went toward Olympus, delighting in their beautiful voices,
their divine song. The dark earth rang around them
as they sang, and a lovely beat rose beneath their feet
as they went to their father, Zeus, who rules in heaven,
himself holding the thunder and the smoking lightning bolt.
By strength he defeated his father Cronus, then set everything
in good order for the immortal gods and assigned their honors.
These things the Muses sang, whose homes are on Olympus,
nine daughters born to mighty Zeus:
Clio, Euterpe, Thalia, Melpomene,
Terpsichore, Erato, Polyhymnia, Urania,
and Calliope, the foremost of them all.

notes.label: Muses
notes.general: Nine goddesses who inspire song and poetry.
notes.here: They sing, dance, and praise the gods.

notes.label: Graces
notes.general: Goddesses of beauty, charm, and delight.
notes.here: They live beside the Muses.

notes.label: Himeros
notes.general: The god who represents desire and longing.
notes.here: He lives near the Muses and the Graces.

notes.label: Olympus
notes.general: The mountain where the gods have their homes.
notes.here: The Muses travel there to their father.

notes.label: Zeus
notes.general: King of the gods and god of thunder and lightning.
notes.here: The Muses’ father, who assigns the gods their honors.

notes.label: Cronus
notes.general: Zeus’s father, who ruled before him.
notes.here: Zeus defeats him by force.

notes.label: Clio
notes.general: One of the nine Muses.
notes.here: The first Muse named in the list.

notes.label: Euterpe
notes.general: One of the nine Muses.
notes.here: She joins her sisters in their song.

notes.label: Thalia
notes.general: One of the nine Muses.
notes.here: She joins her sisters in their song.

notes.label: Melpomene
notes.general: One of the nine Muses.
notes.here: She joins her sisters in their song.

notes.label: Terpsichore
notes.general: One of the nine Muses.
notes.here: She joins her sisters in their song.

notes.label: Erato
notes.general: One of the nine Muses.
notes.here: She joins her sisters in their song.

notes.label: Polyhymnia
notes.general: One of the nine Muses.
notes.here: She joins her sisters in their song.

notes.label: Urania
notes.general: One of the nine Muses.
notes.here: She joins her sisters in their song.

notes.label: Calliope
notes.general: One of the nine Muses.
notes.here: Hesiod calls her the foremost of the sisters.

notes.label: Immortal
notes.general: Living forever, unable to die.
notes.here: A description of the gods.

notes.label: Honors
notes.general: Recognized status, privileges, and responsibilities.
notes.here: Each god receives a particular place and role from Zeus.

passages.title: Their gift to rulers
passages.summary: The Muses give chosen kings the words to judge fairly and settle quarrels.

verses.text: For Calliope also walks beside respected kings.
Whichever king the daughters of mighty Zeus choose to honor
and watch over at birth, among the kings sustained by Zeus,
they pour sweet dew upon his tongue,
and gentle words flow from his mouth. The people
all look to him as he settles disputes
with fair judgments. Speaking with confidence,
he can swiftly and skillfully end even a bitter quarrel.
For this is why kings are wise: for people
who have been wronged, they set matters right in the assembly
with ease, winning them over with gentle words.
As such a king walks through the gathering, people greet him like a god
with warm respect, and he stands out among the crowd.
Such is the Muses’ sacred gift to human beings.

notes.label: Calliope
notes.general: The foremost of the nine Muses.
notes.here: She accompanies respected kings.

notes.label: Muses
notes.general: Goddesses who inspire song and poetry.
notes.here: They also give kings persuasive speech.

notes.label: Zeus
notes.general: King of the gods and father of the Muses.
notes.here: He supports the kings described in the poem.

notes.label: Sweet dew
notes.general: Dew is the moisture that gathers in tiny drops.
notes.here: The Muses pour it onto a king’s tongue as an image of their gift of pleasing speech.

notes.label: Public assembly
notes.general: A gathering where a community discusses public matters.
notes.here: The king settles disputes before the people.

passages.title: Their gift to singers
passages.summary: The Muses and Apollo give people music and song. A singer’s song can make someone forget their grief.

verses.text: For from the Muses and Apollo, who shoots from afar,
come singers and lyre players on earth,
and from Zeus come kings. Fortunate is anyone the Muses
love: sweet speech flows from his mouth.
For though someone bears sorrow in a spirit newly struck by grief
and wastes away, wounded at heart, if a singer,
a servant of the Muses, sings the glorious deeds of people long ago
and the blessed gods whose home is Olympus,
he soon forgets his sadness, and none of his troubles
stay in his mind. So quickly do the goddesses’ gifts turn his thoughts away.

notes.label: Muses
notes.general: Goddesses who inspire poetry, song, and other arts.
notes.here: They give singers their gifts, and their songs bring relief from grief.

notes.label: Apollo
notes.general: A god associated with music and archery.
notes.here: He gives people music along with the Muses. “Who shoots from afar” refers to his skill with a bow.

notes.label: Lyre
notes.general: A stringed instrument played by plucking, often used to accompany singing.
notes.here: Lyre players receive their gifts from the Muses and Apollo.

notes.label: Zeus
notes.general: The king of the Greek gods.
notes.here: Kings owe their position and authority to him.

notes.label: Olympus
notes.general: A mountain in Greece regarded as the home of the gods.
notes.here: The singer celebrates the gods who live there.

notes.label: Blessed
notes.general: Enjoying happiness and good fortune.
notes.here: The word describes the gods’ happy existence.

passages.title: Tell me what came first
passages.summary: Hesiod asks the Muses how the world and the gods began, and what came first.

verses.text: Greetings, daughters of Zeus! Give me a song that stirs longing.
Celebrate the sacred family of the immortal gods who live forever,
those born of Gaia, the Earth, and starry Uranus, the Sky,
and of dark Night, and those whom Pontus, the salty Sea, brought up.
Tell how, in the beginning, the gods and the earth came into being,
and the rivers and the boundless sea, surging with waves,
and the shining stars and the wide sky above,
[and the gods born from these, the givers of good things.]
Tell how they divided their riches and shared out their honors,
and how they first took possession of Olympus with its many ridges.
Tell me these things, Muses whose homes are on Olympus,
from the beginning, and tell me which of them came into being first.

notes.label: Zeus
notes.general: King of the gods.
notes.here: The father of the Muses whom Hesiod addresses.

notes.label: Muses
notes.general: Nine goddesses who inspire song and poetry.
notes.here: Hesiod asks them to tell him how everything began.

notes.label: Gaia
notes.general: Earth herself, understood as a goddess.
notes.here: An ancestor of the gods.

notes.label: Uranus
notes.general: The Sky, understood as a god.
notes.here: The starry Sky from whom gods were born.

notes.label: Night
notes.general: Night herself, understood as a goddess, also called Nyx.
notes.here: Another ancestor of the gods.

notes.label: Pontus
notes.general: The Sea, understood as a god.
notes.here: He brings up some of the gods.

notes.label: Honors
notes.general: Status, privileges, and responsibilities.
notes.here: The gods share these out among themselves.

notes.label: Olympus
notes.general: The mountain home of the gods.
notes.here: Hesiod asks how the gods first came to possess it.

passages.title: The first beings
passages.summary: The first beings appear. Darkness and Night come from Chaos; Night and Darkness become the parents of bright air and Day.

verses.text: First of all Chaos, the vast gap, came into being, and then
broad-chested Gaia, Earth, forever the firm seat of all
the immortals who hold the peak of snowy Olympus,
and misty Tartarus in the depths of Earth with her wide paths,
and Eros, Desire, most beautiful among the immortal gods,
who loosens limbs and, in every god and every human,
overpowers the mind and careful judgment within the heart.
From Chaos came Erebus, Darkness, and black Night.
From Night in turn came Aether, the bright upper air, and Day,
whom she conceived and bore after joining with Erebus in love.

notes.label: Chaos
notes.general: The name means a gap or chasm, rather than everyday disorder.
notes.here: Chaos is the first being to appear and the source of Darkness and Night.

notes.label: Gaia
notes.general: Earth herself, imagined as a goddess.
notes.here: Her broad body provides a firm seat for everything.

notes.label: Tartarus
notes.general: A deep, dark region far below the earth.
notes.here: It appears among the earliest beings, in the earth’s depths.

notes.label: Eros
notes.general: The divine power of love and sexual desire.
notes.here: His power weakens limbs and overwhelms clear thinking in gods and humans alike.

notes.label: Erebus
notes.general: Darkness imagined as a divine being.
notes.here: He comes from Chaos and fathers Aether and Day with Night.

notes.label: Night
notes.general: Night imagined as a goddess, also called Nyx.
notes.here: She comes from Chaos and gives birth to Aether and Day.

notes.label: Aether
notes.general: The bright, clear upper air above the lower atmosphere.
notes.here: Aether is a child of Night and Erebus.

notes.label: Day
notes.general: Daylight imagined as a goddess, also called Hemera.
notes.here: She is born to Night and Erebus.

notes.label: Immortal
notes.general: Living forever; unable to die.
notes.here: The word describes the gods.

passages.title: Earth, Sky, and the Titans
passages.summary: Earth gives birth to Sky, the Mountains, and Sea. With Sky, she then has twelve children. The youngest, Cronus, hates his father.

verses.text: First Gaia, Earth, gave birth to one equal to herself in size,
starry Uranus, Sky, to cover her on every side
and be a firm seat forever for the blessed gods.
She bore the tall Mountains, lovely homes for goddesses,
the Nymphs who live among the mountains and their valleys.
She also bore the barren sea, raging with waves,
Pontus, without the pleasures of love. Then
she lay with Sky and bore Oceanus with his deep whirlpools,
and Coeus, Crius, Hyperion, and Iapetus,
and Theia, Rhea, Themis, and Mnemosyne,
and Phoebe with her golden crown, and lovely Tethys.
After them the youngest was born, Cronus with his crooked schemes,
the most fearsome of her children. He hated his vigorous father.

notes.label: Uranus
notes.general: Sky himself, imagined as a god.
notes.here: Earth bears him and later has children with him.

notes.label: Nymphs
notes.general: Goddesses associated with natural places such as mountains, woods, and springs.
notes.here: These Nymphs live among mountain valleys.

notes.label: Pontus
notes.general: The Sea itself, imagined as a god.
notes.here: Earth gives birth to him without a partner.

notes.label: Barren sea
notes.general: Land is called barren when it produces no crops.
notes.here: The phrase pictures the sea as a place where no harvest grows.

notes.label: Oceanus
notes.general: The god of the great river imagined as surrounding the world; one of the gods called Titans.
notes.here: Earth and Sky’s child, described as having deep whirlpools.

notes.label: Coeus
notes.general: One of the Titans, the twelve children listed here of Earth and Sky.
notes.here: Hesiod names him without describing him further.

notes.label: Crius
notes.general: One of the Titans, children of Earth and Sky.
notes.here: He appears among the brothers born before Cronus.

notes.label: Hyperion
notes.general: One of the Titans, children of Earth and Sky.
notes.here: Hesiod lists him among their sons.

notes.label: Iapetus
notes.general: One of the Titans, children of Earth and Sky.
notes.here: He is another of Cronus’s older brothers.

notes.label: Theia
notes.general: One of the female Titans, daughters of Earth and Sky.
notes.here: She begins the list of their six daughters.

notes.label: Rhea
notes.general: One of the female Titans, daughters of Earth and Sky.
notes.here: She is named alongside her sisters.

notes.label: Themis
notes.general: A Titan goddess associated with justice and the proper order of things.
notes.here: She is listed as a daughter of Earth and Sky.

notes.label: Mnemosyne
notes.general: The goddess of memory and one of the Titans.
notes.here: She is a daughter of Earth and Sky.

notes.label: Phoebe
notes.general: One of the female Titans, daughters of Earth and Sky.
notes.here: She wears a golden crown.

notes.label: Tethys
notes.general: One of the female Titans, daughters of Earth and Sky.
notes.here: Hesiod describes her as lovely.

notes.label: Cronus
notes.general: The youngest Titan, a son of Earth and Sky.
notes.here: He is fearsome, skilled in crooked schemes, and hostile to his father.

passages.title: The Cyclopes and the Hundred-Handers
passages.summary: Earth bears three one-eyed makers of thunder and lightning. Earth and Sky also have three huge sons, each with a hundred hands and fifty heads.

verses.text: Earth also bore the Cyclopes, with their fierce hearts,
Brontes, Steropes, and mighty-hearted Arges,
who gave Zeus his thunder and made his thunderbolt.
In every other way they were like the gods,
but a single eye lay in the middle of each forehead.
They were named Cyclopes, meaning Round-eyes, because
a single round eye lay in each one's forehead.
Strength, force, and skill showed in everything they made.
Then Earth and Sky had three more children,
huge and powerful, too terrible to name,
Cottus, Briareus, and Gyges, towering sons.
A hundred hands sprang from the shoulders of each,
monstrous hands, and each had fifty heads
growing from his shoulders above his sturdy limbs.
Their huge bodies held boundless, mighty strength.

notes.label: Cyclopes
notes.general: One-eyed giants; their name means “Round-eyes.” A single one is a Cyclops.
notes.here: These three brothers are powerful craftspeople who make Zeus’s thunderbolt.

notes.label: Brontes
notes.general: One of the three Cyclopes; his name is connected with thunder.
notes.here: He helps provide Zeus with thunder and a thunderbolt.

notes.label: Steropes
notes.general: One of the three Cyclopes; his name is connected with lightning.
notes.here: He works alongside Brontes and Arges.

notes.label: Arges
notes.general: One of the three Cyclopes; his name suggests brightness or a flash.
notes.here: Hesiod describes him as mighty-hearted.

notes.label: Zeus
notes.general: The god of thunder and lightning, who becomes ruler of the gods.
notes.here: The poem briefly looks ahead to the Cyclopes giving him his weapons.

notes.label: Thunderbolt
notes.general: A bolt of lightning imagined as a weapon.
notes.here: The Cyclopes make it for Zeus.

notes.label: Hundred-Handers
notes.general: A common name for Cottus, Briareus, and Gyges.
notes.here: Each brother has a hundred hands, fifty heads, and immense strength.

notes.label: Cottus
notes.general: One of the three Hundred-Handers, sons of Earth and Sky.
notes.here: He is named first among these enormous brothers.

notes.label: Briareus
notes.general: One of the three Hundred-Handers, sons of Earth and Sky.
notes.here: Like his brothers, he has a hundred hands and fifty heads.

notes.label: Gyges
notes.general: One of the three Hundred-Handers, sons of Earth and Sky.
notes.here: He shares his brothers’ huge size and boundless strength.

passages.title: Earth plans to stop Sky
passages.summary: Sky traps his children inside Earth. In pain, she makes a sickle and asks them to help punish him. Only Cronus agrees, and Earth is delighted.

verses.text: For all the children born to Earth and Sky
were the most fearsome of children, and their father hated them
from the start. As soon as each was born,
he hid them all away and let none come into the light,
deep in a hollow inside Earth. He delighted in this cruel work,
did Sky, while huge Earth groaned within,
cramped by the burden, and thought up a cunning, harmful plan.
Quickly she created gray adamant, a substance of great hardness,
and made a great sickle, then explained her plan to her dear children.
With an aching heart, she spoke to give them courage:
“Children of mine and of a reckless father, if you are willing
to listen to me, we could make your father pay for his cruel abuse.
He was the first to plot these shameful deeds.”
So she spoke. Fear seized them all, and none of them
said a word. But great Cronus, with his crooked schemes, took courage
and answered his loving mother:
“Mother, I promise I can carry out this
deed, for I care nothing for our father
with his shameful name. He was the first to plot these shameful deeds.”
So he spoke, and huge Earth's heart filled with joy.

notes.label: Earth and Sky
notes.general: Gaia and Uranus are both parts of the world and divine parents.
notes.here: Sky forces their children to stay inside Earth, causing her pain.

notes.label: Adamant
notes.general: An extraordinarily hard substance in ancient stories; its exact material is uncertain.
notes.here: Earth creates gray adamant and uses it to make a sickle.

notes.label: Sickle
notes.general: A tool with a curved blade, normally used to cut crops.
notes.here: Earth makes a large one as part of her plan against Sky.

notes.label: Cronus
notes.general: The youngest Titan, a son of Earth and Sky, known for cunning.
notes.here: He alone speaks up and promises to carry out Earth’s plan.

notes.label: Make him pay
notes.general: Punish someone for harm they have caused.
notes.here: Earth asks her children to help punish their father for trapping them inside her.

passages.title: Cronus strikes; new beings arise
passages.summary: Cronus cuts off his father Sky’s genitals. The blood falls on Earth, who later gives birth to spirits of vengeance, Giants, and ash-tree spirits.

verses.text: Gaia, Earth, hid her son Cronus in ambush and placed in his hands
a jagged-toothed sickle, then told him the whole plan.
Then mighty Uranus, Sky, came bringing night, and over Earth,
longing for lovemaking, he settled and stretched himself
in every direction. From his hiding place, his son reached out
with his left hand; with his right he seized the enormous sickle,
long and jagged-toothed, and his own father's genitals
he swiftly sliced away, flinging them back
behind him. They did not leave his hand in vain:
every drop of blood that scattered
Earth caught, and as the years rolled round,
she bore the mighty Erinyes, spirits of vengeance, and the great Giants,
gleaming in armor, holding long spears in their hands,
and the nymphs called Meliae, ash-tree spirits, across the boundless earth.

notes.label: Gaia
notes.general: Earth herself, imagined as a goddess.
notes.here: She hides Cronus, gives him the weapon, and receives Sky’s blood.

notes.label: Cronus
notes.general: A divine son of Earth and Sky.
notes.here: He attacks his father from a hiding place.

notes.label: Uranus
notes.general: Sky himself, imagined as a god; his Greek name is Ouranos.
notes.here: He spreads over Earth and is attacked by his son.

notes.label: Sickle
notes.general: A curved blade usually used to cut crops.
notes.here: Cronus uses a huge version with a jagged cutting edge.

notes.label: Genitals
notes.general: The external sexual organs.
notes.here: Cronus cuts off his father’s genitals and throws them behind him.

notes.label: Erinyes
notes.general: Goddesses of vengeance, also called the Furies.
notes.here: Earth gives birth to them after receiving Sky’s blood.

notes.label: Giants
notes.general: A race of powerful beings born from Earth.
notes.here: They appear as warriors with shining armor and long spears.

notes.label: Meliae
notes.general: Nymphs, or female nature spirits, associated with ash trees.
notes.here: They too are born from Earth after Sky’s blood falls on her.

passages.title: Aphrodite rises from the sea
passages.summary: Aphrodite grows in sea foam around Sky’s severed genitals. Love and Desire accompany her, and she receives power over attraction, pleasure, and lovemaking.

verses.text: Once Cronus had cut off the genitals with adamant, an unbreakable material,
and thrown them from the land into the surging sea,
they drifted over the water for a long time. White
foam rose around the immortal flesh, and within it a girl
grew. First she drew near holy Cythera,
then from there she reached Cyprus, surrounded by the sea.
Out stepped a beautiful goddess, worthy of reverence, and grass
grew beneath her slender feet. They call her Aphrodite,
the foam-born goddess and Cytherea of the lovely crown,
gods and humans alike, because she grew in foam, called aphros in Greek;
and Cytherea because she came to Cythera;
and Cyprus-born because she was born on wave-washed Cyprus;
and Genital-loving because she appeared from genitals.
Eros, Love, went with her, and beautiful Himeros, Desire, followed
from her birth, as she went to join the company of gods.
From the beginning, Aphrodite has held this honor and been allotted
this share among humans and immortal gods:
young women's intimate whispers, smiles and deceptions,
sweet pleasure, lovemaking, and tenderness.

notes.label: Adamant
notes.general: A legendary substance imagined as extraordinarily hard.
notes.here: It is the material of Cronus’s cutting blade.

notes.label: Aphrodite
notes.general: The goddess of love, sexual attraction, and pleasure.
notes.here: She grows in sea foam and steps ashore on Cyprus.

notes.label: Aphros
notes.general: The Greek word for foam.
notes.here: Hesiod uses its sound to explain Aphrodite’s name.

notes.label: Cythera / Cytherea
notes.general: Cythera is an island south of mainland Greece; Cytherea means “goddess of Cythera.”
notes.here: Aphrodite approaches this holy island before reaching Cyprus.

notes.label: Cyprus / Cyprus-born
notes.general: Cyprus is an island in the eastern Mediterranean.
notes.here: Hesiod connects Aphrodite’s title “Cyprus-born” with her birth and arrival there.

notes.label: Genital-loving
notes.general: A startling divine nickname built around a Greek word for genitals.
notes.here: Hesiod connects the nickname with the body parts from which Aphrodite appeared.

notes.label: Eros
notes.general: Love, especially sexual attraction, imagined as a god.
notes.here: He accompanies Aphrodite from her birth.

notes.label: Himeros
notes.general: Longing or desire, imagined as a god.
notes.here: He follows Aphrodite as she joins the gods.

passages.title: Sky names the Titans
passages.summary: Sky calls his children Titans, blaming their reckless act and warning that they will pay for it.

verses.text: Their father gave these children the name Titans,
mighty Uranus, Sky, rebuking those he himself had fathered.
He said they had strained in their recklessness to do a monstrous
deed, and punishment for it would come in time.

notes.label: Titans
notes.general: A generation of gods born from Earth and Sky, including Cronus.
notes.here: Sky uses the name as an accusation. Hesiod links its sound with Greek words for straining and punishment.

notes.label: Reproach
notes.general: Words expressing blame or strong disapproval.
notes.here: Sky gives his children their name while condemning what they have done.

passages.title: The children of Night
passages.summary: Night gives birth on her own to many divine beings, including Death, Sleep, Dreams, the Fates, and Strife.

verses.text: Night bore hateful Moros, Doom, and black Ker, a spirit of death,
and Thanatos, Death; she bore Hypnos, Sleep, and the tribe of Dreams.
The dark goddess Night bore them without sleeping with anyone.
Then she bore Momus, Blame, and Oizys, painful Misery,
and the Hesperides, who tend, beyond the famed river Oceanus,
the beautiful golden apples and the trees that bear that fruit.
She also bore the Fates and the Keres, merciless avengers,
Clotho, Lachesis, and Atropos, who give mortals
their share of good and bad when they are born,
and pursue the wrongdoing of humans and gods.
These goddesses never let their terrible anger rest
until they make whoever has done wrong pay dearly.
Deadly Night also bore Nemesis, Payback, a scourge to mortal humans;
after Nemesis she bore Apate, Deceit, and Philotes, Intimacy,
and destructive Old Age, and Eris, fierce-hearted Strife.

notes.label: Night
notes.general: Night herself, imagined as a goddess; her Greek name is Nyx.
notes.here: She produces these children without a sexual partner.

notes.label: Moros
notes.general: Doom or an unavoidable fate, imagined as a divine being.
notes.here: He is Night’s first child named in this list.

notes.label: Ker / Keres
notes.general: Ker is a spirit of death or fatal doom; Keres is the plural.
notes.here: A single black Ker appears first; later the Keres appear as merciless avengers.

notes.label: Thanatos
notes.general: Death himself, imagined as a god.
notes.here: He is a child of Night and a brother of Sleep.

notes.label: Hypnos
notes.general: Sleep himself, imagined as a god.
notes.here: Night bears him alongside Death and the Dreams.

notes.label: Dreams
notes.general: Dreams imagined as a family of divine beings.
notes.here: Night gives birth to their whole tribe.

notes.label: Momus
notes.general: Blame or fault-finding, imagined as a god.
notes.here: He is one of Night’s children.

notes.label: Oizys
notes.general: Misery or distress, imagined as a goddess.
notes.here: Hesiod describes her as painful.

notes.label: Hesperides
notes.general: Divine maidens associated with the evening and the far west.
notes.here: They tend golden apples and the trees that grow them.

notes.label: Oceanus
notes.general: The great river believed to circle the world, also imagined as a god.
notes.here: The Hesperides care for their trees beyond it.

notes.label: Fates
notes.general: Goddesses who assign each person’s lot in life; their Greek name is Moirai.
notes.here: They give people good and bad at birth and appear alongside powers that punish wrongdoing.

notes.label: Clotho
notes.general: One of the three named Fates; her name means “Spinner.”
notes.here: She is named with Lachesis and Atropos among those who assign people their lot.

notes.label: Lachesis
notes.general: One of the three named Fates; her name means “Allotter.”
notes.here: She helps assign the good and bad people receive in life.

notes.label: Atropos
notes.general: One of the three named Fates; her name means “Unturning” or “Unchangeable.”
notes.here: She appears with Clotho and Lachesis.

notes.label: Nemesis
notes.general: A goddess of resentment and deserved payback for wrongdoing.
notes.here: Night bears her as a source of suffering for mortals.

notes.label: Apate
notes.general: Deceit imagined as a goddess.
notes.here: She is born after Nemesis.

notes.label: Philotes
notes.general: Affection or intimacy, including sexual intimacy, imagined as a goddess.
notes.here: She is another child of Night.

notes.label: Old Age
notes.general: Old age imagined as a divine being, called Geras in Greek.
notes.here: Hesiod calls it destructive.

notes.label: Eris
notes.general: Strife or conflict imagined as a goddess.
notes.here: She is Night’s fierce-hearted child.

passages.title: The children of Strife
passages.summary: Strife gives birth to suffering, violence, lies and other troubles. A knowingly false oath brings especially great harm.

verses.text: Then hateful Strife gave birth to painful Toil,
Forgetfulness and Hunger, and Sorrows that bring tears;
Clashes and Battles, Murders and Slaughter;
Quarrels, lying Words and Arguments;
Lawlessness and Ruin, always close companions;
and Oath, who brings the worst suffering to people on earth
whenever someone knowingly swears a false oath.

notes.label: Strife
notes.general: Conflict and hostility, imagined as a goddess.
notes.here: She gives birth to the troubles listed here.

notes.label: Toil
notes.general: Hard, exhausting work.
notes.here: Painful Toil is one of Strife’s children.

notes.label: Troubles as children
notes.general: A poem can turn an idea or experience into a living being.
notes.here: Hunger, Lies and the other troubles become members of a divine family.

notes.label: Lawlessness
notes.general: Disregard for laws and proper behavior.
notes.here: Lawlessness and Ruin are close companions.

notes.label: Ruin
notes.general: Disaster, including the reckless blindness that can lead to it.
notes.here: Strife’s daughter Ruin stays close to Lawlessness.

notes.label: Oath
notes.general: A solemn promise or claim, made with divine powers as witnesses.
notes.here: Oath becomes a divine being who punishes deliberate false swearing.

passages.title: The sea god Nereus
passages.summary: The Sea fathers honest, gentle Nereus. With Earth, he also has Thaumas, Phorcys, Ceto and strong-hearted Eurybia.

verses.text: Pontus, the Sea, fathered Nereus, truthful and free from lies,
the eldest of his children. They call him the Old Man
because he is trustworthy and gentle, and never forgets
what is right, but has thoughts that are fair and kind.
Pontus also fathered mighty Thaumas and proud Phorcys
by mating with Gaia, the Earth, and Ceto with her lovely cheeks,
and Eurybia, whose heart is as hard as unbreakable stone.

notes.label: Pontus
notes.general: The Sea imagined as a god.
notes.here: He fathers Nereus and, with Gaia, four more children.

notes.label: Nereus
notes.general: A gentle, truthful sea god, often called the Old Man of the Sea.
notes.here: He is Pontus’s eldest child and always respects what is right.

notes.label: Gaia
notes.general: The Earth imagined as a goddess.
notes.here: She and Pontus are the parents of Thaumas, Phorcys, Ceto and Eurybia.

notes.label: Thaumas
notes.general: A divine son of Sea and Earth.
notes.here: He is described as mighty.

notes.label: Phorcys
notes.general: A sea god, born from Sea and Earth.
notes.here: He is described as proud.

notes.label: Ceto
notes.general: A sea goddess, born from Sea and Earth.
notes.here: The poem praises her lovely cheeks.

notes.label: Eurybia
notes.general: A goddess, born from Sea and Earth.
notes.here: Her hard, unyielding spirit is compared to unbreakable stone.

passages.title: The daughters of Nereus
passages.summary: Nereus and Doris have fifty sea-goddess daughters. Some calm waves and winds; all are skilled at their work.

verses.text: Nereus had dearly loved daughters, all goddesses,
in the sea that yields no harvest, with lovely-haired Doris,
daughter of Oceanus, the great river:
Ploto, Eucrante, Sao and Amphitrite;
Eudora, Thetis, Galene and Glauce;
Cymothoe, Speio, Thoe and lovely Halia;
Pasithea, Erato and Eunice with her rosy arms;
graceful Melite, Eulimene and Agave;
Doto, Proto, Pherusa and Dynamene;
Nesaea, Actaea and Protomedea;
Doris, Panopea and beautiful Galatea;
lovely Hippothoe and Hipponoe with her rosy arms;
and Cymodoce, who calms the waves on the misty sea
and the blasts of raging winds, with Cymatolege
and Amphitrite of the lovely ankles, doing so with ease;
Cymo, Eione and Halimede with her lovely crown;
Glauconome, who loves to smile, and Pontoporea;
Leagora, Euagora and Laomedea;
Polynoe, Autonoe and Lysianassa;
Euarne, lovely in figure and flawless in looks;
Psamathe with her graceful body, and glorious Menippe;
Neso, Eupompe, Themisto and Pronoe;
and Nemertes, who has her immortal father’s mind.
These daughters were born to faultless Nereus,
fifty in all, and all knew how to do their work without fault.

notes.label: Nereids
notes.general: The fifty sea-goddess daughters of Nereus and Doris.
notes.here: The poem names all fifty and praises their beauty and skill.

notes.label: Nereus
notes.general: The truthful, gentle sea god introduced just before this passage.
notes.here: He is the father of all fifty daughters.

notes.label: Doris, the mother
notes.general: A goddess who is a daughter of Oceanus.
notes.here: She and Nereus are the parents of the fifty sea goddesses.

notes.label: Oceanus
notes.general: The divine river imagined as flowing around the world.
notes.here: He is Doris’s father and the daughters’ grandfather.

notes.label: The sea that yields no harvest
notes.general: A poetic description of the sea, where people cannot grow crops.
notes.here: It sets the daughters’ home apart from cultivated land.

notes.label: Amphitrite
notes.general: One of the fifty sea goddesses.
notes.here: She helps Cymodoce and Cymatolege calm waves and winds.

notes.label: Thetis
notes.general: One of Nereus and Doris’s sea-goddess daughters.
notes.here: She appears near the beginning of the list.

notes.label: Doris, the daughter
notes.general: One of the fifty sea goddesses.
notes.here: She shares her name with her mother.

notes.label: Galatea
notes.general: One of the fifty sea goddesses.
notes.here: The poem singles out her beauty.

notes.label: Cymodoce
notes.general: A sea goddess whose name is connected with waves.
notes.here: She calms waves and fierce winds with two of her sisters.

notes.label: Cymatolege
notes.general: A sea goddess whose name suggests stilling waves.
notes.here: She helps Cymodoce and Amphitrite calm the sea.

notes.label: Rosy arms
notes.general: Arms whose beauty or color is compared to roses.
notes.here: The description praises Eunice and Hipponoe.

notes.label: Nemertes
notes.general: One of the fifty sea goddesses.
notes.here: She shares the mind of her truthful father, Nereus.

passages.title: Iris and the Gorgons
passages.summary: Electra gives birth to Iris and the Harpies. Ceto gives birth to the gray-haired Graiae and the Gorgons. When Perseus cuts off Medusa's head, Chrysaor and Pegasus spring out. Pegasus flies to the gods and carries Zeus's thunder and lightning.

verses.text: Thaumas took as his wife the daughter of deep-flowing Oceanus,
Electra, who gave birth to swift Iris
and the lovely-haired Harpies, Aello and Ocypete,
who keep pace with gusts of wind and birds
on their swift wings, darting high through the air.
Ceto bore to Phorcys the fair-cheeked Graiae,
gray-haired from birth. That is why they are called Graiae, the Old Women,
by the immortal gods and humans who walk the earth:
Pemphredo in her lovely robe and Enyo in her saffron-yellow robe.
Ceto also bore to Phorcys the Gorgons, who live beyond famous Oceanus,
at the world's far edge toward Night, where the clear-voiced Hesperides live:
Sthenno, Euryale, and Medusa, who suffered a terrible fate.
Medusa was mortal; the others were immortal and ageless,
both of them. Dark-haired Poseidon lay with Medusa
in a soft meadow among spring flowers.
When Perseus cut off Medusa's head,
great Chrysaor and the horse Pegasus sprang out.
Pegasus took his name from the springs of Oceanus, where
he was born; Chrysaor was named for the golden sword he held in his hands.
Pegasus flew away, leaving the earth, mother of flocks,
and reached the immortal gods. He lives in Zeus's halls,
carrying thunder and lightning for Zeus, the wise planner.

notes.label: Thaumas
notes.general: A sea god.
notes.here: Electra's husband and father of Iris and the Harpies.

notes.label: Oceanus
notes.general: The divine river imagined as flowing around the world.
notes.here: Electra's father; the Gorgons live beyond his waters.

notes.label: Electra
notes.general: A divine daughter of Oceanus.
notes.here: Mother of Iris and the Harpies.

notes.label: Iris
notes.general: A goddess associated with the rainbow and a messenger for the gods.
notes.here: The swift daughter of Thaumas and Electra.

notes.label: Harpies
notes.general: Winged female beings whose name suggests snatching things away.
notes.here: Their wings carry them as fast as winds and birds.

notes.label: Aello
notes.general: A Harpy whose name suggests a storm wind.
notes.here: One of Electra's two Harpy daughters.

notes.label: Ocypete
notes.general: A Harpy whose name means “swift-flying.”
notes.here: Aello's sister.

notes.label: Ceto
notes.general: A sea goddess.
notes.here: Mother of the Graiae and the Gorgons.

notes.label: Phorcys
notes.general: A sea god.
notes.here: Father of Ceto's children.

notes.label: Graiae
notes.general: Their Greek name means “Old Women.”
notes.here: Hesiod explains their name through their gray hair, which they had from birth.

notes.label: Pemphredo
notes.general: One of the Graiae.
notes.here: She wears a beautiful robe.

notes.label: Enyo
notes.general: One of the Graiae; a different figure from the war goddess with the same name.
notes.here: She wears a saffron-yellow robe.

notes.label: Saffron-yellow
notes.general: A rich golden yellow, like the color made from saffron spice.
notes.here: The color of Enyo's robe.

notes.label: Gorgons
notes.general: Three fearsome sisters: Sthenno, Euryale, and Medusa.
notes.here: They live beyond Oceanus, near Night.

notes.label: Night
notes.general: Hesiod treats Night as a divine being.
notes.here: Her region marks the remote place where the Gorgons live.

notes.label: Hesperides
notes.general: Divine maidens associated with evening and the far west.
notes.here: Their clear voices are heard in the region where the Gorgons live.

notes.label: Sthenno
notes.general: One of the three Gorgons.
notes.here: She is immortal and never grows old.

notes.label: Euryale
notes.general: One of the three Gorgons.
notes.here: Like Sthenno, she is immortal and never grows old.

notes.label: Medusa
notes.general: The only mortal Gorgon.
notes.here: Perseus cuts off her head, and Chrysaor and Pegasus emerge.

notes.label: Poseidon
notes.general: The god of the sea, often called “the Dark-haired One.”
notes.here: He sleeps with Medusa in a meadow.

notes.label: Perseus
notes.general: A Greek hero.
notes.here: He kills Medusa by cutting off her head.

notes.label: Chrysaor
notes.general: His name means “Golden Sword.”
notes.here: He emerges from Medusa holding a golden sword, which explains his name.

notes.label: Pegasus
notes.general: A winged horse. Hesiod links his name with pēgai, the Greek word for “springs.”
notes.here: Born beside Oceanus's springs, he flies to the gods and carries Zeus's thunder and lightning.

notes.label: Zeus
notes.general: King of the gods, associated with thunder and lightning.
notes.here: Pegasus lives in his halls and carries his thunder and lightning.

passages.title: Geryon and Echidna
passages.summary: Heracles kills three-headed Geryon and takes his cattle. Echidna, half beautiful nymph and half terrifying snake, lives forever in a cave underground.

verses.text: Chrysaor fathered three-headed Geryon
after mating with Callirhoe, daughter of famous Oceanus.
Mighty Heracles killed Geryon
beside his shambling cattle on Erytheia, surrounded by water,
on the day he drove the broad-browed cattle
to sacred Tiryns, crossing the stream of Oceanus,
after killing Orthus and Eurytion the cattle herder
in their misty cattle shelter beyond famous Oceanus.
Ceto bore another monster, impossible to overcome, nothing like
mortal humans or the deathless gods:
divine, fierce-hearted Echidna, born in a hollow cave,
half a bright-eyed nymph with lovely cheeks,
and half a monstrous snake, dreadful and huge,
with dappled skin, eating raw flesh in the depths of sacred earth.
There her cave lies deep beneath a hollow rock,
far from deathless gods and mortal humans.
There the gods assigned her a splendid home to live in.
There dreadful Echidna stays underground in the land of the Arimoi,
a nymph who never dies or grows old, through all her days.

notes.label: Chrysaor
notes.general: A mythical figure whose name means “Golden Sword.”
notes.here: He fathers Geryon with Callirhoe.

notes.label: Geryon
notes.general: A three-headed being who owns a herd of cattle.
notes.here: Heracles kills him and drives away his cattle.

notes.label: Callirhoe
notes.general: A daughter of the river god Oceanus.
notes.here: She is Geryon’s mother.

notes.label: Oceanus
notes.general: The divine river imagined as flowing around the world.
notes.here: Heracles crosses his stream to bring the cattle home.

notes.label: Heracles
notes.general: A Greek hero famous for his enormous strength; also called Hercules.
notes.here: He kills Geryon, Orthus, and Eurytion and takes the cattle.

notes.label: Erytheia
notes.general: A mythical island beyond Oceanus.
notes.here: Geryon and his cattle are there.

notes.label: Tiryns
notes.general: An ancient Greek city associated with Heracles.
notes.here: Heracles brings the cattle to this sacred city.

notes.label: Orthus
notes.general: Geryon’s monstrous watchdog.
notes.here: Heracles kills him at the cattle shelter.

notes.label: Eurytion
notes.general: The herder who looks after Geryon’s cattle.
notes.here: Heracles kills him alongside Orthus.

notes.label: Echidna
notes.general: An immortal creature, half woman and half snake.
notes.here: She lives underground, far from gods and humans.

notes.label: Nymph
notes.general: A female divine spirit connected with nature.
notes.here: Echidna’s upper half looks like a beautiful nymph.

notes.label: Arimoi
notes.general: A people or region whose location is uncertain.
notes.here: Echidna’s underground home is in their land.

passages.title: Echidna's fearsome children
passages.summary: Echidna’s family includes terrifying dogs, the Hydra, and other monsters. Heroes defeat several of them. Ceto and Phorcys also have a snake that guards golden apples.

verses.text: They say Typhaon joined in love with Echidna,
he, terrible, violent and lawless, with that bright-eyed girl.
She became pregnant and bore fierce-hearted children.
First she bore Orthus, a dog for Geryon;
second she bore a monster beyond words, impossible to overcome:
Cerberus, the raw-flesh-eating dog of Hades, with a voice like bronze,
with fifty heads, merciless and strong.
Third she bore the Hydra, skilled in deadly harm,
the water snake of Lerna, whom white-armed Hera raised,
her anger at mighty Heracles knowing no bounds.
But Zeus's son killed the Hydra with pitiless bronze,
Amphitryon's son, together with Iolaus, who loved battle,
Heracles, guided by Athena, bringer of spoils.
Echidna also bore the Chimera, breathing unstoppable fire,
dreadful and huge, swift-footed and strong.
She had three heads: one a fierce-eyed lion's,
one a goat's, and one a snake's, a mighty serpent's.
A lion in front, a serpent behind, a goat in the middle,
she breathed out the dreadful force of blazing fire.
Pegasus and brave Bellerophon brought her down.
Echidna bore the deadly Sphinx, a curse on the people of Thebes,
after mating with Orthus, and also the lion of Nemea.
Hera, Zeus's glorious wife, raised the lion
and settled him in Nemea's hills, a curse on humans.
Living there, he ravaged the local people,
ruling over Tretus, Nemea and Apesas.
But mighty Heracles overpowered him with his strength.
Ceto joined in love with Phorcys and bore her youngest child,
a dreadful snake that, in the hidden depths of dark earth,
at its vast outer limits, guards the all-golden apples.
Such are the offspring of Ceto and Phorcys.

notes.label: Typhaon
notes.general: A powerful monstrous being, also called Typhon.
notes.here: He mates with Echidna and fathers her first children.

notes.label: Orthus
notes.general: The monstrous dog that guards Geryon’s cattle.
notes.here: He is Echidna’s first child and later fathers two monsters.

notes.label: Cerberus
notes.general: The dog of the underworld, where the dead go.
notes.here: Hesiod gives him fifty heads and a voice like bronze.

notes.label: Hades
notes.general: The god who rules the dead; his name can also mean his realm.
notes.here: Cerberus is his dog.

notes.label: Hydra of Lerna
notes.general: A dangerous water monster associated with Lerna in Greece.
notes.here: Hera raises her, and Heracles kills her with help.

notes.label: Hera
notes.general: A major goddess and the wife of Zeus.
notes.here: She raises the Hydra out of hatred for Heracles and also raises the Nemean lion.

notes.label: Heracles
notes.general: A famously strong hero, born to Zeus and a human mother.
notes.here: He defeats the Hydra and the Nemean lion.

notes.label: Zeus
notes.general: The chief Greek god.
notes.here: He is Heracles’s father and Hera’s husband.

notes.label: Amphitryon
notes.general: The human husband of Heracles’s mother.
notes.here: Heracles is called his son as well as Zeus’s son.

notes.label: Iolaus
notes.general: A companion of Heracles.
notes.here: He helps Heracles kill the Hydra.

notes.label: Athena
notes.general: A goddess of wisdom, skilled action, and warfare.
notes.here: Her guidance helps Heracles defeat the Hydra.

notes.label: Bronze
notes.general: A metal used for ancient weapons, armor, and other objects.
notes.here: It describes Cerberus’s ringing voice and stands for Heracles’s weapon.

notes.label: Chimera
notes.general: A fire-breathing monster combining different animals.
notes.here: She has the heads of a lion, a goat, and a snake.

notes.label: Pegasus and Bellerophon
notes.general: Pegasus is a winged horse; Bellerophon is a human hero.
notes.here: Together they defeat the Chimera.

notes.label: Sphinx
notes.general: A female monster associated with the Greek city of Thebes.
notes.here: She brings destruction to its people, called Cadmeans in the Greek.

notes.label: Nemean lion
notes.general: A monstrous lion associated with Nemea in Greece.
notes.here: He terrorizes the surrounding area until Heracles defeats him.

notes.label: Tretus, Nemea, and Apesas
notes.general: Neighboring places in Greece: a mountain pass, a valley, and a mountain.
notes.here: They mark the territory dominated by the lion.

notes.label: Ceto and Phorcys
notes.general: Ancient sea divinities who are parents of several monsters.
notes.here: Their youngest child is the snake guarding the golden apples.

notes.label: Golden apples
notes.general: Precious mythical fruit kept at the far edge of the world.
notes.here: A dreadful snake guards them; this passage gives the snake no name.

passages.title: Rivers born of Ocean
passages.summary: Tethys and Ocean have many sons, the river gods.

verses.text: Tethys bore Ocean the swirling Rivers:
Nile, Alpheus, and Eridanus with his deep whirlpools;
Strymon, Maeander, and Ister with his lovely streams;
Phasis, Rhesus, and Achelous with his silver swirls;
Nessus, Rhodius, Haliacmon, and Heptaporus;
Grenicus, Aesepus, and sacred Simois;
Peneus, Hermus, and Caicus with his fine-flowing waters;
great Sangarius, Ladon, and Parthenius;
Evenus, Ardescus, and sacred Scamander.

notes.label: Tethys
notes.general: A Titan goddess and the mother of rivers and water goddesses.
notes.here: She bears Ocean these river sons.

notes.label: Ocean
notes.general: Ocean, or Oceanus, is the god of the great river believed to circle the world.
notes.here: He is the father of the Rivers.

notes.label: Rivers
notes.general: For the Greeks, a river could also be a god.
notes.here: The named rivers are children of Tethys and Ocean.

notes.label: Nile
notes.general: The great river of Egypt.
notes.here: One of the river sons.

notes.label: Alpheus
notes.general: A river in southern Greece, flowing past Olympia.
notes.here: One of the river sons.

notes.label: Eridanus
notes.general: A mythical river whose location was understood differently by different ancient writers.
notes.here: His waters form deep whirlpools.

notes.label: Strymon
notes.general: A river flowing into the northern Aegean Sea.
notes.here: One of the river sons.

notes.label: Maeander
notes.general: A famously winding river in what is now western Turkey.
notes.here: One of the river sons.

notes.label: Ister
notes.general: The ancient Greek name for the Danube.
notes.here: Hesiod praises his lovely streams.

notes.label: Phasis
notes.general: A river at the eastern end of the Black Sea, in what is now Georgia.
notes.here: One of the river sons.

notes.label: Rhesus
notes.general: A river name associated with the region around Troy.
notes.here: One of the river sons.

notes.label: Achelous
notes.general: A major river in western Greece and its god.
notes.here: His swirling waters gleam like silver.

notes.label: Nessus
notes.general: A river name in Hesiod’s list.
notes.here: One of the river sons.

notes.label: Rhodius
notes.general: A river in the region around Troy.
notes.here: One of the river sons.

notes.label: Haliacmon

notes.here: One of the river sons.

notes.label: Heptaporus

notes.here: One of the river sons.

notes.label: Grenicus

notes.here: One of the river sons.

notes.label: Aesepus

notes.here: One of the river sons.

notes.label: Simois
notes.general: A river near Troy.
notes.here: Hesiod calls him sacred.

notes.label: Peneus
notes.general: A major river in Thessaly, in Greece.
notes.here: One of the river sons.

notes.label: Hermus
notes.general: A river in what is now western Turkey.
notes.here: One of the river sons.

notes.label: Caicus
notes.general: A river in what is now western Turkey.
notes.here: Hesiod praises his flowing waters.

notes.label: Sangarius
notes.general: A large river in what is now Turkey.
notes.here: Hesiod calls him great.

notes.label: Ladon
notes.general: A river in Arcadia, in southern Greece.
notes.here: One of the river sons.

notes.label: Parthenius

notes.label: Evenus
notes.general: A river in western Greece.

notes.label: Ardescus
notes.general: A river name in Hesiod’s list.
notes.here: One of the river sons.

notes.label: Scamander
notes.general: A river near Troy, also worshipped as a god.
notes.here: Hesiod calls him sacred.

passages.title: The daughters of Ocean
passages.summary: Ocean and Tethys have three thousand daughters who care for the young and watch over land and water. They also have just as many river sons.

verses.text: Tethys also bore a sacred family of daughters, who across the earth
nurture boys to manhood, together with Lord Apollo
and the Rivers. This is the task Zeus has given them:
Peitho, Admete, Ianthe, Electra,
Doris, Prymno, and godlike Urania;
Hippo, Clymene, Rhodea, Callirhoe;
Zeuxo, Clytie, Idyia, Pasithoe;
Plexaura, Galaxaura, and lovely Dione;
Melobosis, Phoe, and beautiful Polydora;
Cerceis, lovely in form, and wide-eyed Pluto;
Perseis, Ianeira, Acaste, Xanthe;
lovely Petraea, Menestho, Europa;
Metis, Eurynome, and Telesto in her saffron-colored robe;
Chryseis, Asia, and enchanting Calypso;
Eudora, Tyche, Amphiro, Ocyroe;
and Styx, the foremost of them all.
These daughters were born to Ocean and Tethys,
the eldest of their daughters, but there are many others.
For there are three thousand slender-ankled daughters of Ocean,
scattered far and wide, watching over the earth and the waters' depths
everywhere alike, glorious children of goddesses.
And there are just as many Rivers, flowing with a roar,
sons of Ocean, whom noble Tethys bore.
It would be hard for a mortal to tell all their names,
but those who live beside each river know its name.

notes.label: Daughters of Ocean
notes.general: These water goddesses are often called Oceanids.
notes.here: Hesiod names the eldest, then says there are three thousand altogether.

notes.label: Apollo
notes.general: A god associated with music, prophecy, healing, and the protection of the young.
notes.here: He helps the Rivers and Ocean’s daughters nurture the young.

notes.label: Zeus

notes.here: He assigns the daughters their task.

notes.label: Peitho

notes.label: Metis
notes.general: A goddess of wisdom and clever planning.
notes.here: One of Ocean and Tethys’s eldest daughters.

notes.label: Eurynome
notes.general: An Oceanid who is also the mother of the Graces.
notes.here: One of Ocean and Tethys’s eldest daughters.

notes.label: Telesto
notes.general: One of the Oceanids, the water goddesses.
notes.here: She wears a saffron-colored robe.

notes.label: Saffron-colored
notes.general: A rich yellow or orange-yellow, like the color produced by saffron dye.
notes.here: The color of Telesto’s robe.

notes.label: Chryseis
notes.general: An Oceanid who shares her name with a woman in the story of the Trojan War.
notes.here: A daughter of Ocean and Tethys.

notes.label: Asia
notes.general: One of the Oceanids, the water goddesses.
notes.here: A goddess’s name, rather than a place in this sentence.

notes.label: Calypso
notes.general: A goddess whose parentage differs across Greek poems.
notes.here: Hesiod makes her Ocean and Tethys’s daughter and calls her enchanting.

notes.label: Eudora
notes.general: One of the Oceanids, the water goddesses.
notes.here: One of the eldest daughters.

notes.label: Tyche
notes.general: The goddess of fortune or chance.
notes.here: One of Ocean and Tethys’s eldest daughters.

notes.label: Amphiro
notes.general: One of the Oceanids, the water goddesses.
notes.here: One of the eldest daughters.

notes.label: Ocyroe
notes.general: One of the Oceanids, the water goddesses.
notes.here: One of the eldest daughters.

notes.label: Styx
notes.general: A goddess and an underworld river whose water seals the gods’ most binding oaths.
notes.here: Hesiod ranks her foremost among Ocean’s daughters.

notes.label: Mortal
notes.general: Someone who will eventually die, especially a human.
notes.here: A human could hardly name every river.

passages.title: Sun, Moon, and Dawn
passages.summary: Theia and Hyperion have three children: Sun, Moon, and Dawn.

verses.text: Theia bore great Helios, the Sun, and bright Selene, the Moon,
and Eos, the Dawn, who shines for everyone on earth
and for the immortal gods who dwell in the wide sky,
having yielded to Hyperion in love.

notes.label: Theia
notes.general: One of the Titans, an older generation of gods.
notes.here: The mother of Helios, Selene, and Eos.

notes.label: Hyperion
notes.general: One of the Titans.
notes.here: The father of Helios, Selene, and Eos.

notes.label: Helios
notes.general: The Sun as a god.
notes.here: Theia and Hyperion’s son.

notes.label: Selene
notes.general: The Moon as a goddess.
notes.here: Theia and Hyperion’s bright daughter.

notes.label: Eos
notes.general: The goddess of dawn, the first light of morning.
notes.here: She brings light to people and gods.

notes.label: Immortal
notes.general: Living forever; unable to die.
notes.here: A description of the gods.

passages.title: Winds and stars
passages.summary: Eurybia and Crius have three sons. Eos and one of those sons, Astraeus, become the parents of the Winds and stars.

verses.text: Eurybia, shining among goddesses, joined Crius in love and bore him
great Astraeus, Pallas,
and Perses, whose knowledge set him apart from all others.
Eos bore Astraeus the fierce-hearted Winds:
Zephyrus, who clears the sky, and swift-moving Boreas,
and Notus, after lying with him in love, goddess with god.
After the Winds, Eos, born at daybreak, bore Eosphorus, the Morning Star,
and the gleaming stars that crown the sky.

notes.label: Eurybia
notes.general: A goddess, daughter of Earth and the Sea.
notes.here: With Crius, she has Astraeus, Pallas, and Perses.

notes.label: Crius
notes.general: One of the Titans, an older generation of gods.
notes.here: The father of Astraeus, Pallas, and Perses.

notes.label: Astraeus
notes.general: A god associated with stars.
notes.here: With Eos, he fathers the Winds and stars.

notes.label: Pallas
notes.general: A god who shares his name with other mythical figures.
notes.here: A son of Eurybia and Crius.

notes.label: Perses
notes.general: A son of Eurybia and Crius.
notes.here: Hesiod singles him out for his knowledge.

notes.label: Eos
notes.general: The goddess of dawn.
notes.here: She is the mother of the Winds and stars; “born at daybreak” is a poetic title for her.

notes.label: Winds
notes.general: The Greeks imagined winds as gods with their own names and characters.
notes.here: Three are named as children of Eos and Astraeus.

notes.label: Zephyrus
notes.general: The god of the west wind.
notes.here: He is described as clearing the sky.

notes.label: Boreas
notes.general: The god of the north wind.
notes.here: He travels swiftly.

notes.label: Notus
notes.general: The god of the south wind.
notes.here: The third Wind named.

notes.label: Eosphorus
notes.general: The Morning Star: the planet Venus when it appears before sunrise.
notes.here: A divine child of Eos and Astraeus.

passages.title: Styx stands with Zeus
passages.summary: Styx and her children support Zeus. He rewards them and keeps his promises to the other gods.

verses.text: Styx, Oceanus’s daughter, joined in love with Pallas and bore
Zelos and Nike of the lovely ankles in their halls.
She also bore Kratos and Bia, her glorious children.
They have no home, no seat apart from Zeus,
and take no road unless the god leads them.
They always sit beside Zeus, whose thunder crashes loud.
For this was what deathless Styx, Oceanus’s daughter, had planned
on the day when Zeus, the lightning-flinger of Olympus,
called all the immortal gods to high Olympus.
He said that any god who fought beside him against the Titans
would lose none of their privileges; each would keep the honor
they had held before among the immortal gods.
And anyone without honor or privilege under Cronus, he said,
would gain both honor and privileges, as was their right.
Deathless Styx was the first to come to Olympus,
bringing her children, following her dear father’s advice.
Zeus honored her and gave her exceptional gifts.
He made her the great oath by which the gods swear,
and gave her children a home beside him for all time.
Just so, he fulfilled his promises to all the gods,
every one. He himself holds mighty power and rules.

notes.label: Styx
notes.general: A goddess and a river whose water makes the gods’ most binding oath.
notes.here: She brings her children to support Zeus.

notes.label: Oceanus
notes.general: The god of the great river believed to circle the world.
notes.here: Styx’s father, who advises her to join Zeus.

notes.label: Pallas
notes.general: A god from the Titan family.
notes.here: The father of Styx’s four children.

notes.label: Zelos
notes.general: The spirit of rivalry and the drive to excel.
notes.here: One of Styx’s children, always beside Zeus.

notes.label: Nike
notes.general: The goddess of victory.
notes.here: One of Styx’s children, described as having lovely ankles.

notes.label: Kratos
notes.general: The spirit of power and might.
notes.here: One of Styx’s children, always beside Zeus.

notes.label: Bia
notes.general: The spirit of force.
notes.here: One of Styx’s children, always beside Zeus.

notes.label: Zeus
notes.general: The god of thunder and lightning, who becomes ruler of the gods.
notes.here: He promises rewards to the gods who fight beside him.

notes.label: Olympus
notes.general: The mountain home of the gods.
notes.here: Zeus gathers the gods there.

notes.label: Titans
notes.general: An older generation of gods.
notes.here: Zeus calls for allies to fight against them.

notes.label: Cronus
notes.general: Zeus’s father, who ruled the gods before him.
notes.here: Zeus offers honor to gods who had received none under Cronus.

notes.label: Honor and privileges
notes.general: A god’s recognized rank, rights, and share of power.
notes.here: Zeus promises to protect or grant these.

notes.label: Oath
notes.general: A solemn promise that binds the person making it.
notes.here: The gods swear their strongest oath by Styx.

passages.title: Hecate's family
passages.summary: Phoebe has two daughters, Leto and Asteria. Asteria’s daughter Hecate receives great honors from Zeus.

verses.text: Phoebe in turn came to Coeus’s bed of delight.
The goddess conceived in love with the god
and bore Leto in her dark-blue robe, always gentle,
kind to humans and immortal gods,
gentle from the very first, the kindest on Olympus.
Phoebe also bore renowned Asteria, whom Perses once
brought to his great house to be called his dear wife.
Asteria conceived and bore Hecate, whom
Zeus, Cronus’s son, honored above all and gave splendid gifts:
a share of the earth and the unharvested sea.

notes.label: Phoebe
notes.general: A goddess of the older Titan generation.
notes.here: The mother of Leto and Asteria.

notes.label: Coeus
notes.general: A god of the older Titan generation.
notes.here: The father of Phoebe’s daughters.

notes.label: Leto
notes.general: A goddess, later the mother of Apollo and Artemis.
notes.here: Phoebe’s gentle daughter, dressed in dark blue.

notes.label: Asteria
notes.general: A goddess, the sister of Leto.
notes.here: Perses’s wife and Hecate’s mother.

notes.label: Perses
notes.general: A god from the Titan family.
notes.here: Asteria’s husband and Hecate’s father.

notes.label: Hecate
notes.general: A goddess with powers reaching across earth, sea, and heaven.
notes.here: Zeus grants her a share of earth and sea.

notes.label: Zeus
notes.general: The ruler of the gods and son of Cronus.
notes.here: He gives Hecate exceptional honor.

notes.label: Cronus
notes.general: Zeus’s father and the gods’ earlier ruler.
notes.here: He is named to identify Zeus’s family.

notes.label: Olympus
notes.general: The mountain home of the gods.
notes.here: Leto is called the kindest there.

notes.label: Unharvested sea
notes.general: A traditional poetic description of the sea, often understood as bearing no crops.
notes.here: The sea is one of the realms in which Hecate receives a share.

passages.title: The honors Hecate keeps
passages.summary: Hecate keeps her ancient powers and honors. She can answer prayers and give people success and prosperity.

verses.text: Hecate also has a share of honor in starry heaven,
and the immortal gods honor her greatly.
For even now, whenever someone living on earth
seeks divine favor with fine offerings, as custom requires,
they call on Hecate. Great honor comes
with ease to anyone whose prayers the goddess gladly accepts.
She grants them prosperity too, for she has the power.
Of all the gods born from Gaia and Uranus
who received honor, Hecate has a portion of every one’s share.
Zeus, Cronus’s son, neither forced her aside nor took away
anything she received among the Titans, the earlier gods.
She keeps her share as it was allotted at the very beginning.
Though an only child, the goddess has no smaller share of honor
or privilege on earth, in heaven, and at sea,
but far more still, because Zeus honors her.

notes.label: Hecate
notes.general: A goddess whose powers extend across earth, sea, and heaven.
notes.here: She keeps her earlier rights and can grant blessings to people.

notes.label: Offerings
notes.general: Gifts or sacrifices presented to a god.
notes.here: People make them while asking for divine favor.

notes.label: Prosperity
notes.general: Wealth, success, and a flourishing life.
notes.here: A blessing Hecate has the power to give.

notes.label: Gaia
notes.general: Earth herself, understood as a goddess.
notes.here: With Uranus, she is the parent of the older gods.

notes.label: Uranus
notes.general: Sky himself, understood as a god.
notes.here: With Gaia, he is the parent of the older gods.

notes.label: Zeus
notes.general: The ruler of the gods.
notes.here: He protects Hecate’s earlier privileges and gives her great honor.

notes.label: Cronus
notes.general: Zeus’s father and the gods’ earlier ruler.
notes.here: Zeus is identified as his son.

notes.label: Titans
notes.general: The older generation of gods descended from Gaia and Uranus.
notes.here: Hecate already held privileges among them before Zeus ruled.

notes.label: Share of honor
notes.general: An allotted part of divine authority, rank, and privileges.
notes.here: Hecate shares in the powers assigned to the older gods.

passages.title: Where Hecate helps
passages.summary: Hecate can help people in public life, war, sports, fishing, and farming. She also cares for the young.

verses.text: Hecate stands beside whoever she chooses and gives them powerful help.
In the public assembly, she makes whoever she favors stand out.
And whenever men arm themselves for war that destroys lives,
the goddess stands beside those she chooses,
eager to grant them victory and glory.
She sits beside respected kings as they give judgment.
She is a good helper, too, when men compete in games:
there the goddess stands beside them and lends her aid.
The winner, victorious through might and strength, wins a fine prize
and carries it off with ease and joy, bringing glory to his parents.
She is good at helping riders, too, whenever she chooses.
And for those who work the gray, rough sea
and pray to Hecate and the thundering Earth-shaker, Poseidon,
the glorious goddess easily grants a great catch,
and easily takes it away when it comes in sight, if her heart desires.
With Hermes, she is good at making livestock thrive in their pens.
Herds of cattle and great herds of goats,
and flocks of woolly sheep, if her heart desires,
she makes grow from few to many, or dwindle from many to few.
So, though Hecate is her mother's only child,
she holds honored privileges among all the immortal gods.
Zeus, the son of Cronus, made her nurse of the young who, after her,
opened their eyes to the light of far-seeing Dawn.
So from the beginning she has nursed the young. These are her honors.

notes.label: Hecate
notes.general: A goddess with powers over many parts of life.
notes.here: She chooses whom to help and can give success or take it away.

notes.label: Public assembly
notes.general: A gathering where a community discusses public matters.
notes.here: Hecate can make a person stand out among the speakers and listeners.

notes.label: Earth-shaker
notes.general: A name for Poseidon, god of the sea and earthquakes.
notes.here: People fishing at sea pray to him along with Hecate.

notes.label: Hermes
notes.general: A god associated with travel, messages, and livestock.
notes.here: He and Hecate help herds and flocks grow.

notes.label: Zeus
notes.general: The son of Cronus who becomes ruler of the gods.
notes.here: He gives Hecate the task of caring for the young.

notes.label: Dawn
notes.general: Eos, the goddess who brings the morning light.
notes.here: Seeing Dawn's light means coming into the world alive.

passages.title: Cronus swallows his children
passages.summary: Cronus learns that his son will overthrow him. He swallows his children as they are born, leaving Rhea in lasting grief.

verses.text: Rhea lay with Cronus and bore glorious children:
Hestia, Demeter, and Hera with her golden sandals;
mighty Hades, who lives in halls beneath the earth
with a pitiless heart; and the thundering Earth-shaker, Poseidon;
and Zeus, wise in planning, father of gods and humans,
whose thunder makes the wide earth shake.
Great Cronus swallowed them, each one
as it came from its mother's sacred womb to her knees.
His purpose was to keep any other glorious descendant of Uranus
from holding royal honor among the immortal gods.
For he had learned from Gaia and starry Uranus
that he was destined to be overcome by his own son,
strong though he was, through the plans of great Zeus.
So Cronus kept a sharp watch, and as he waited,
he swallowed his own children. Rhea was gripped by grief that would not fade.

notes.label: Rhea
notes.general: A daughter of Gaia and Uranus, and Cronus's partner.
notes.here: She is the mother of the six gods named in this passage.

notes.label: Cronus
notes.general: A son of Gaia and Uranus who rules the gods before Zeus.
notes.here: He swallows his children to prevent one of them from taking his power.

notes.label: Hestia
notes.general: The goddess of the hearth, the fire at the center of a home.
notes.here: She is one of Rhea and Cronus's daughters.

notes.label: Demeter
notes.general: A goddess of grain and farming.
notes.here: She is one of Rhea and Cronus's daughters.

notes.label: Hera
notes.general: A goddess of marriage who becomes queen of the gods.
