notes.here: She is a daughter of Rhea and Cronus, pictured wearing golden sandals.

notes.label: Hades
notes.general: The god who rules the world of the dead beneath the earth.
notes.here: His underground home and pitiless heart mark his stern power.

notes.label: Poseidon
notes.general: The god of the sea and earthquakes, also called Earth-shaker.
notes.here: He is one of Rhea and Cronus's sons.

notes.label: Zeus
notes.general: The god of thunder who becomes ruler of the gods.
notes.here: He is the son whose plans will bring about Cronus's defeat. “Father of gods and humans” is a title of authority.

notes.label: Gaia
notes.general: Earth herself, a goddess and the mother of Cronus and Rhea.
notes.here: She tells Cronus that his own son will overcome him.

notes.label: Uranus
notes.general: Sky himself, a god and the father of Cronus and Rhea.
notes.here: He and Gaia reveal Cronus's fate. Cronus's children are also his descendants.

passages.title: Rhea hides Zeus
passages.summary: Rhea asks her parents to help save her next baby. She gives birth to Zeus on Crete, where he is hidden in a cave.

verses.text: But when Rhea was about to bear Zeus, father of gods and humans,
she begged her own dear parents,
Gaia and starry Uranus,
to help her devise a plan so she could give birth in secret
to her dear child and win vengeance for her father
and for the children great Cronus, with his crooked schemes, had swallowed.
Gaia and Uranus listened closely to their dear daughter and agreed to help.
They told her all that fate had in store
for King Cronus and his strong-hearted son.
They sent her to Lyctus, in the fertile land of Crete,
when she was about to bear her youngest child,
great Zeus. Vast Gaia received him from her
to nourish and care for him on the broad island of Crete.
Gaia came there carrying him through the swift, black night,
first to Lyctus. Taking him in her arms, she hid him
in a deep cave, in the hidden places of the holy earth,
on Mount Aegeum, thickly covered with forest.

notes.label: Rhea
notes.general: Cronus's partner and the mother of his children.
notes.here: She seeks a way to save her youngest child, Zeus.

notes.label: Gaia and Uranus
notes.general: Earth and Sky, the parents of Rhea and Cronus.
notes.here: They help Rhea plan Zeus's secret birth, and Gaia receives him into her care.

notes.label: Cronus
notes.general: The ruler of the gods before Zeus.
notes.here: Rhea seeks revenge for his swallowing their children and for his earlier attack on his father, Uranus.

notes.label: Zeus
notes.general: The youngest child of Rhea and Cronus, destined to rule the gods.
notes.here: His mother hides him so Cronus cannot swallow him.

notes.label: Lyctus
notes.general: An ancient town on Crete, a large Greek island.
notes.here: Rhea's parents send her there for Zeus's birth.

notes.label: Mount Aegeum
notes.general: The mountain on Crete named here as Zeus's hiding place.
notes.here: Its thick forest and deep cave shelter the baby.

passages.title: The stone and the return of Zeus's family
passages.summary: Cronus brings his swallowed children back up. Zeus sets up the stone as a lasting sign and frees his uncles, who give him thunder and lightning.

verses.text: Rhea wrapped a great stone in baby clothes and handed it
to Cronus, son of Ouranos, the mighty lord who then ruled the gods.
He took it in his hands and swallowed it into his belly,
the ruthless creature. He never realized that, left behind,
his own son, unconquerable and untroubled, was safe in place of the stone,
and would soon overpower him with his strength and his own hands,
drive him from his royal honors, and himself rule among the immortals.
Then the young lord Zeus's strength and splendid limbs
grew swiftly. As the years rolled on,
tricked by Gaia's deeply knowing advice,
great Cronus, with his crooked schemes, brought his children back up,
overcome by the cunning and strength of his own son.
First he vomited out the stone he had swallowed last.
Zeus set it firmly in the earth with its broad roads,
at holy Pytho, in the valleys beneath Parnassus,
to stand as a sign for ages to come, a wonder for mortal people.
Zeus freed his father's brothers from their terrible chains,
the sons of Ouranos, whom their father had recklessly bound.
They remembered his kindness and repaid his good deeds:
they gave him thunder and the smoking thunderbolt
and lightning, which vast Gaia had kept hidden until then.
Trusting in these weapons, Zeus rules over mortals and immortals.

notes.label: Rhea
notes.general: A goddess, the wife of Cronus and mother of Zeus.
notes.here: She gives Cronus a wrapped stone in place of baby Zeus.

notes.label: Cronus
notes.general: A Titan, son of Ouranos and Gaia, and father of Zeus.
notes.here: He rules the gods and has swallowed his children to prevent them from replacing him.

notes.label: Ouranos
notes.general: The god who is the sky.
notes.here: He is the father of Cronus and of the brothers Zeus frees.

notes.label: Zeus
notes.general: The god who becomes ruler of gods and humans.
notes.here: He survives Cronus’s attempt to swallow him and gains thunder and lightning.

notes.label: Gaia
notes.general: The goddess who is the earth.
notes.here: Her advice helps bring Cronus’s children back. She has also kept the thunder and lightning hidden.

notes.label: Pytho
notes.general: An older name for Delphi, a sacred place in Greece.
notes.here: Zeus sets up the stone there as a lasting sign.

notes.label: Parnassus
notes.general: A mountain above Delphi.
notes.here: It locates the place where Zeus sets up the stone.

notes.label: Zeus’s father’s brothers
notes.general: The Cyclopes, divine craftsmen with one eye each, are sons of Ouranos and Gaia.
notes.here: These are the uncles who repay Zeus with thunder, the thunderbolt, and lightning.

notes.label: Thunderbolt
notes.general: A bolt of lightning imagined as a weapon a god can throw.
notes.here: Hesiod describes it as smoking and names it alongside thunder and lightning.

passages.title: The sons of Iapetus
passages.summary: Iapetus and Clymene have four sons. Epimetheus brings humans trouble, Zeus strikes down Menoetius, and Atlas must hold up the sky.

verses.text: Iapetus took as his wife a daughter of Oceanus with lovely ankles,
Clymene, and went to bed with her.
She bore him a son, Atlas, strong in spirit,
and Menoetius, full of overbearing pride, and Prometheus,
clever and endlessly inventive, and Epimetheus, whose thinking went astray.
From the start, Epimetheus brought trouble to people who live on bread:
he was the first to welcome the woman Zeus had fashioned,
a virgin. As for violent Menoetius, Zeus, whose gaze reaches far,
struck him with a smoking thunderbolt and sent him down into Erebus,
because of his recklessness and overpowering arrogance.
Atlas holds up the broad sky under harsh compulsion,
at the ends of the earth, before the clear-voiced Hesperides,
standing with the weight on his head and tireless hands.
This was the fate Zeus, the wise planner, assigned him.

notes.label: Iapetus
notes.general: A Titan, one of the older generation of gods.
notes.here: He and Clymene are the parents of the four brothers.

notes.label: Clymene
notes.general: A goddess, daughter of Oceanus.
notes.here: She marries Iapetus and gives birth to Atlas, Menoetius, Prometheus, and Epimetheus.

notes.label: Oceanus
notes.general: The god of the great river imagined as surrounding the earth.
notes.here: He is Clymene’s father.

notes.label: Atlas
notes.general: A son of Iapetus and Clymene.
notes.here: Zeus makes him hold up the sky with his head and hands.

notes.label: Menoetius
notes.general: A brother of Atlas, Prometheus, and Epimetheus.
notes.here: Zeus strikes him down for his reckless arrogance.

notes.label: Prometheus
notes.general: A god known for his clever schemes.
notes.here: Hesiod introduces his inventive mind before describing his punishment.

notes.label: Epimetheus
notes.general: A brother of Prometheus whose judgment fails him.
notes.here: He accepts the woman made at Zeus’s command, bringing trouble to humans.

notes.label: The girl Zeus had made
notes.general: The first woman, known elsewhere as Pandora.
notes.here: Hesiod leaves her unnamed. Zeus has her made, and Epimetheus welcomes her.

notes.label: Erebus
notes.general: The dark region beneath the earth.
notes.here: Zeus sends Menoetius down into it.

notes.label: Hesperides
notes.general: Divine sisters associated with the far west and the guarding of golden apples.
notes.here: Their clear voices and distant home help describe where Atlas stands.

passages.title: Prometheus is bound
passages.summary: An eagle eats Prometheus’s liver every day, and it grows back each night. With Zeus’s consent, Heracles kills the eagle and ends Prometheus’s suffering.

verses.text: Zeus bound Prometheus, with all his intricate schemes, in inescapable
and painful chains, driving a pillar through his middle.
He set a long-winged eagle on him, and it ate his liver,
which could not die. The liver grew back fully
each night, as much as the wide-winged bird had eaten all day.
Heracles, mighty son of Alcmene with her lovely ankles,
killed the eagle and drove that cruel affliction
away from Prometheus, son of Iapetus, freeing him from his suffering,
with the consent of Zeus, who rules on high from Olympus,
so that the fame of Heracles, born in Thebes, would grow
still greater than before across the earth that feeds so many.
Out of regard for this, Zeus honored his glorious son.
Angry though he was, Zeus gave up the anger he had long held
because Prometheus had matched wits with him, the mighty son of Cronus.

notes.label: Prometheus
notes.general: A son of Iapetus, known for his cleverness.
notes.here: Zeus punishes him for challenging his plans.

notes.label: Immortal liver
notes.general: The liver is an organ inside the body. Immortal means unable to die.
notes.here: Prometheus’s liver grows back each night, allowing the eagle’s attack to happen again each day.

notes.label: Heracles
notes.general: A mighty hero, son of Zeus and the human woman Alcmene. Also called Hercules.
notes.here: He kills the eagle, ending Prometheus’s torment and increasing his own fame.

notes.label: Alcmene
notes.general: The mother of Heracles.
notes.here: Hesiod describes her as having lovely ankles.

notes.label: Olympus
notes.general: The mountain that is the home of Zeus and other gods.
notes.here: It identifies Zeus’s place of rule.

notes.label: Thebes
notes.general: A city in Greece.
notes.here: It is the birthplace of Heracles.

notes.label: The son of Cronus
notes.general: Another way of naming Zeus through his father.
notes.here: Zeus is the mighty god whose plans Prometheus challenged.

passages.title: Prometheus divides the sacrifice
passages.summary: Prometheus hides bones under tempting fat. Zeus sees through the trick, and trouble will follow for humans. This explains why people burn bones as offerings to the gods.

verses.text: For when gods and mortal humans were settling their dispute
at Mecone, Prometheus eagerly divided a great ox
and set the portions before them, trying to deceive Zeus.
In one portion he placed the meat and the organs rich with fat
inside the hide, covering them with the ox’s stomach;
in the other, he arranged the ox’s white bones with cunning skill
and laid them out, covered with shining fat.
Then the father of gods and humans said to him:
“Son of Iapetus, most glorious of all lords,
my friend, how unevenly you have divided the portions!”
So Zeus mocked him, Zeus whose plans never fail.
Prometheus, with his twisting schemes, answered him
with a gentle smile, still mindful of his cunning trick:
“Zeus, greatest and most glorious of the everlasting gods,
choose whichever portion your heart urges you to take.”
So he spoke deceitfully. But Zeus, whose plans never fail,
recognized the trick and saw it clearly; in his heart he foresaw troubles
for mortal humans, troubles that would indeed come true.
With both hands Zeus lifted the white fat.
Rage filled his mind, and anger reached his heart
when he saw the ox’s white bones laid out in that cunning trick.
Ever since then, the peoples of the earth have offered the immortal gods
white bones burned on altars fragrant with sacrifice.

notes.label: Prometheus
notes.general: A divine figure known for clever schemes and for helping humans.
notes.here: He divides the ox and tries to make the portion of bones look better than the meat.

notes.label: Zeus
notes.general: The ruler of the gods, associated with the sky and thunder.
notes.here: Called the father of gods and humans, he recognizes Prometheus’s trick.

notes.label: Iapetus
notes.general: One of the Titans, an older generation of gods.
notes.here: Prometheus’s father. Zeus addresses Prometheus as “Son of Iapetus.”

notes.label: Mecone
notes.general: An ancient name for Sicyon, a place in Greece.
notes.here: The place where gods and humans meet and Prometheus divides the ox.

notes.label: Sacrifice and altar
notes.general: A sacrifice is an offering to a god. An altar is the structure on which offerings are placed or burned.
notes.here: Hesiod explains the custom of burning an animal’s bones and fat for the gods.

passages.title: Prometheus steals fire
passages.summary: Zeus withholds fire from humans. Prometheus steals it in a hollow stalk, making Zeus furious.

verses.text: Deeply angered, Zeus the cloud-gatherer said to Prometheus:
“Son of Iapetus, clever beyond all others,
my friend, you still have not forgotten your cunning tricks!”
So spoke Zeus in anger, Zeus whose plans never fail.
From then on, always remembering the trick,
he withheld the power of tireless fire in ash wood
from mortal humans who live upon the earth.
But the noble son of Iapetus, Prometheus, deceived him
by stealing the far-shining glow of tireless fire
in a hollow fennel stalk. The theft bit deep into the heart
of Zeus, who thunders on high, and filled his heart with anger
when he saw fire’s far-shining glow among humans.

notes.label: Zeus
notes.general: The ruler of the gods, who controls clouds and thunder.
notes.here: He withholds fire because of Prometheus’s trick with the ox.

notes.label: Prometheus
notes.general: A clever divine figure and a son of the Titan Iapetus.
notes.here: He steals fire and brings it to humans.

notes.label: Ash wood
notes.general: Wood from an ash tree; “ash” here does not mean the powder left after burning.
notes.here: The Greek wording connecting ash trees and fire is uncertain.

notes.label: Fennel stalk
notes.general: Giant fennel has a stalk whose inner material can carry a slowly burning ember.
notes.here: Prometheus uses a hollow stalk to carry the stolen fire.

passages.title: A woman is made
passages.summary: Zeus answers the theft of fire by having a woman made and beautifully dressed. Gods and humans marvel at her, but she is a trap for humans.

verses.text: At once, in return for fire, Zeus made an evil for humans.
For famous Hephaestus, lame in both legs, shaped earth
into the likeness of a modest young woman, following the plan of Zeus, son of Cronus.
The bright-eyed goddess Athena dressed and belted her
in a silvery robe, and over her head she lowered a veil
with her own hands, intricately worked, a wonder to see.
Around her head, garlands of flowers from the fresh-grown grass
were placed by Pallas Athena, lovely garlands.
Athena also placed a golden crown upon her head,
which famous Hephaestus, lame in both legs, had made himself,
working skillfully with his hands to please his father Zeus.
On it were crafted many intricate figures, a wonder to see:
creatures of the many kinds the land and sea sustain.
He set many of these upon it, and great beauty shone from them,
marvelous figures, like living creatures with voices of their own.
When Hephaestus had made this beautiful evil in exchange for the good,
he led her out to where the other gods and humans were,
glorying in the finery given by bright-eyed Athena, daughter of a mighty father.
Wonder seized the immortal gods and mortal humans
when they saw this deadly trap, which humans had no means to escape.

notes.label: Zeus and Cronus
notes.general: Zeus rules the gods. Cronus, a Titan, is his father.
notes.here: “Son of Cronus” means Zeus, who plans the response to the stolen fire.

notes.label: Hephaestus
notes.general: The god of skilled craft and metalworking, traditionally depicted with a disability affecting his legs.
notes.here: He shapes the woman from earth and makes her golden crown.

notes.label: Athena
notes.general: A daughter of Zeus, associated with wisdom, warfare, and skilled crafts.
notes.here: She dresses the woman and places the veil and crown on her.

notes.label: The woman
notes.general: This figure is usually identified as Pandora, who is named in Hesiod’s other poem, Works and Days.
notes.here: Hesiod gives her no personal name in these lines. He presents her beauty as part of Zeus’s trap.

passages.title: Hesiod's judgment on women
passages.summary: Hesiod presents both marriage and staying unmarried as sources of trouble for men. He says no one can escape Zeus’s plans, even Prometheus.

verses.text: From that first woman comes the race of women,
for from her comes the deadly race and the tribes of women,
a great trouble, living among mortal men,
sharing their plenty, but never their ruinous poverty.
Just as bees in their sheltered hives
feed the drones, partners in harmful work,
while the bees, all day until the sun goes down,
hurry about their daily work and build white honeycombs,
the drones stay inside the covered hives
and reap the fruits of others’ toil into their own bellies.
Just so, as a curse for mortal men, women
were made by Zeus, who thunders on high, to share in work
that brings pain. And he gave men another evil in place of a blessing:
a man who shuns marriage and women’s troublesome ways
and chooses never to marry reaches cruel old age
with no one to care for him. He has enough to live on
while he is alive, but when he dies, his property is divided
among distant relatives. And a man whose fate is to marry
and who gets a good wife with sound sense
finds evil competing with good throughout his life,
without a break. But a man who gets a wife of a wicked kind
lives with unending sorrow in his chest,
in his heart and spirit, and there is no cure for that misery.
So no one can deceive the mind of Zeus or escape his plans.
Even kindly Prometheus, son of Iapetus,
did not escape Zeus’s heavy anger. By force,
a mighty chain holds him fast, for all his knowledge.

notes.label: The first woman
notes.general: In this story, the gods make the first woman as part of Zeus’s punishment for humans.
notes.here: “That first woman” refers to the beautiful woman described just before this passage.

notes.label: Drones
notes.general: Drones are male bees. Worker bees build the comb and gather food.
notes.here: Hesiod compares women to drones eating food produced by others. This expresses his hostile view of women.

notes.label: Mortal
notes.general: Someone who will eventually die, unlike an immortal god.
notes.here: The mortal men are human men.

notes.label: Zeus
notes.general: The ruler of the gods, associated with thunder and lightning.
notes.here: Hesiod presents women and the difficulties of marriage as parts of Zeus’s punishment.

notes.label: Prometheus
notes.general: A clever god who challenged Zeus and stole fire for humans.
notes.here: Even his cleverness cannot save him from Zeus’s punishment.

notes.label: Iapetus
notes.general: A Titan and the father of Prometheus.
notes.here: Hesiod identifies Prometheus through his father.

passages.title: The Hundred-Handers are freed
passages.summary: Uranus imprisoned his three powerful sons underground. Gaia tells Zeus and his fellow gods that freeing them will help them win.

verses.text: When their father Uranus first grew angry with Briareus,
Cottus, and Gyges, he bound them in mighty chains,
awed by their overwhelming strength, their appearance,
and their size, and made them live beneath the wide-pathed earth.
There they dwelled beneath the ground in pain,
at the farthest edge, at the limits of the great earth,
suffering for a very long time, with deep grief in their hearts.
But Zeus, son of Cronus, and the other immortal gods,
whom lovely-haired Rhea bore through her love with Cronus,
brought them back into the light on Gaia’s advice.
For Gaia herself had told the gods everything in full:
with these brothers’ help, they would win victory and shining glory.

notes.label: Uranus
notes.general: The god of the sky, Gaia’s partner and the father of many early gods.
notes.here: He imprisons Briareus, Cottus, and Gyges because their strength and size alarm him.

notes.label: Briareus
notes.general: One of three giant brothers called the Hundred-Handers. Each has a hundred hands and fifty heads.
notes.here: He is freed from imprisonment beneath the earth.

notes.label: Cottus
notes.general: One of the three Hundred-Handers, sons of Gaia and Uranus.
notes.here: He has suffered underground with his brothers.

notes.label: Gyges
notes.general: One of the three Hundred-Handers, alongside Briareus and Cottus.
notes.here: He shares his brothers’ imprisonment and release.

notes.label: Zeus
notes.general: A son of Cronus and Rhea who becomes ruler of the gods.
notes.here: He and his fellow gods bring the imprisoned brothers back into the light.

notes.label: Cronus
notes.general: A Titan who ruled the gods before Zeus.
notes.here: He is the father of Zeus and the other gods who free the brothers.

notes.label: Rhea
notes.general: A Titan and the mother of Zeus and his siblings by Cronus.
notes.here: Hesiod describes her as lovely-haired.

notes.label: Gaia
notes.general: Earth herself, understood as a goddess.
notes.here: She advises the gods to free the brothers so they can help win the war.

passages.title: Ten years of war
passages.summary: The Titans and the children of Cronus have fought for ten full years. Neither side is winning.

verses.text: For a long time the two sides had fought, enduring heart-rending toil,
the Titan gods and all the children of Cronus,
facing each other in fierce battles,
the proud Titans fighting from high Mount Othrys,
and from Olympus the gods who give good things,
whom lovely-haired Rhea bore after sharing Cronus’s bed.
With heart-rending anger against each other,
they fought without a break for ten full years.
Neither side could find release or an end to the bitter struggle;
the outcome of the war hung in an even balance.

notes.label: Titans
notes.general: An older generation of gods, born to Gaia and Uranus.
notes.here: The Titans fighting from Mount Othrys oppose Zeus and the other children of Cronus.

notes.label: Cronus
notes.general: A Titan and the father of Zeus and his siblings.
notes.here: His children form the side fighting against the Titans.

notes.label: Mount Othrys
notes.general: A mountain in mainland Greece.
notes.here: It serves as the Titans’ base in the war.

notes.label: Olympus
notes.general: A mountain in Greece associated with the home of Zeus and his fellow gods.
notes.here: The children of Cronus fight from Olympus.

notes.label: Rhea
notes.general: The mother of Zeus and his siblings by Cronus.
notes.here: Her children are the gods fighting from Olympus.

passages.title: Zeus asks for help
passages.summary: Zeus feeds the freed brothers and asks them to help defeat the Titans, reminding them that he and his allies rescued them.

verses.text: But when Zeus had given the three brothers all they needed,
nectar and ambrosia, the food the gods themselves eat,
proud courage grew in all their chests.
Once they had tasted nectar and delicious ambrosia,
Zeus, father of gods and humans, spoke to them:
“Listen to me, glorious children of Gaia and Uranus,
so I can tell you what the heart in my chest urges me to say.
For a very long time now, facing each other,
we have fought day after day for victory and power,
the Titan gods and all of us born to Cronus.
Now show your great strength and your irresistible hands
against the Titans in this grim battle.
Remember our loving kindness: after all your suffering,
you came back into the light, out of those cruel chains,
through our plans, out of the misty darkness.”

notes.label: Zeus
notes.general: The ruler of the gods, often called the father of gods and humans.
notes.here: He feeds the Hundred-Handers and asks them to join his side in the war.

notes.label: Nectar
notes.general: The drink of the gods.
notes.here: Together with ambrosia, it restores the freed brothers’ courage.

notes.label: Ambrosia
notes.general: The food of the gods.
notes.here: Zeus gives it to the brothers after their imprisonment.

notes.label: Gaia
notes.general: Earth herself, understood as a goddess.
notes.here: She is the mother of the three brothers Zeus addresses.

notes.label: Uranus
notes.general: The god of the sky and the father of the Hundred-Handers.
notes.here: Zeus names the brothers’ parents when calling on them.

notes.label: Cronus
notes.general: The father of Zeus and his siblings by Rhea.
notes.here: Zeus identifies his side as the children of Cronus.

notes.label: Titans
notes.general: An older generation of gods.
notes.here: They are the enemies Zeus asks the Hundred-Handers to fight.

passages.title: Cottus answers Zeus
passages.summary: Cottus thanks Zeus for freeing him and his companions. They promise to fight the Titans and defend Zeus and his allies.

verses.text: So Zeus spoke, and noble Cottus answered him:
“Mighty god, what you tell us is no mystery. We ourselves
know how far your wisdom and understanding surpass all others;
you have shielded the immortal gods from chilling ruin.
Thanks to your wise care, out of the misty darkness
and free of merciless chains, back once more
we have come, lord, son of Cronus, after suffering beyond imagining.
So now, with steady minds and careful planning,
we will defend your power in this terrible war,
fighting the Titans through the fiercest battles.”

notes.label: Cottus
notes.general: One of three giant brothers, each with a hundred hands and fifty heads.
notes.here: He speaks for the brothers Zeus has freed from imprisonment.

notes.label: Zeus
notes.general: The god who commands thunder and lightning, and a son of Cronus.
notes.here: Cottus thanks him for freeing the brothers and promises to defend his side.

notes.label: Cronus
notes.general: A Titan and the father of Zeus and several other gods.
notes.here: Cottus addresses Zeus as the son of Cronus.

notes.label: Titans
notes.general: An older generation of gods.
notes.here: The Titans are fighting Zeus and his allies.

notes.label: Immortal
notes.general: Unable to die.
notes.here: The gods can fight and suffer, even though they cannot die.

passages.title: The armies meet
passages.summary: Both armies charge into battle. The hundred-handed giants fight for Zeus, and the violence shakes the sea, earth, sky, and depths below.

verses.text: So Cottus spoke. The gods, the givers of good things, approved
the words they heard, and their hearts longed for war
still more than before. They stirred up a dreadful battle,
all of them, female and male alike, on that day:
the Titan gods, all the children of Cronus,
and those Zeus had brought into the light from Erebus, the darkness beneath the earth,
terrifying, powerful beings with overwhelming strength.
A hundred hands sprang from the shoulders
of every one of them, and each had fifty heads
growing from his shoulders above his sturdy limbs.
These giants now faced the Titans in deadly battle,
holding towering rocks in their powerful hands.
Across from them, the Titans tightened their battle ranks
eagerly, and showed what their hands and strength could do,
as did their foes. The boundless sea roared terribly all around;
the earth crashed aloud, and the wide sky groaned
and shook. Tall Olympus shuddered from its base
under the immortals’ onslaught, and a heavy tremor reached
misty Tartarus, along with the piercing roar of feet
in the endless rush of battle, and the crash of mighty blows.
So they hurled their weapons of pain at one another.
The voices of both sides reached the starry sky
as they called out and clashed with a mighty battle shout.

notes.label: Titans
notes.general: An older generation of gods.
notes.here: They form their ranks against Zeus and his allies.

notes.label: Cronus
notes.general: A Titan and the father of Zeus and several other gods.
notes.here: His children form one of the groups fighting the Titans.

notes.label: Zeus
notes.general: The god who commands thunder and lightning.
notes.here: He has freed the hundred-handed giants to join his side.

notes.label: Erebus
notes.general: The darkness deep beneath the earth.
notes.here: Zeus brought the imprisoned giants out of this darkness into daylight.

notes.label: Hundred-handed giants
notes.general: Cottus, Briareus, and Gyes: three brothers with a hundred hands and fifty heads each.
notes.here: They face the Titans with huge rocks in their hands.

notes.label: Olympus
notes.general: A high mountain associated with the home of the gods.
notes.here: The gods’ assault shakes the mountain from its base.

notes.label: Tartarus
notes.general: A vast, dark region far beneath the earth.
notes.here: Even these depths feel the battle’s tremors and noise.

passages.title: Zeus fills the world with fire
passages.summary: Zeus unleashes all his strength. His lightning burns the world, blinds the Titans, and makes a noise like Earth and Sky crashing together.

verses.text: Now Zeus no longer held back his fury;
at once his heart filled with rage, and he revealed
his full strength. From heaven and Olympus together
he advanced, flashing lightning without a pause. His thunderbolts
flew thick and fast with thunder and lightning
from his powerful hand, whirling sacred flame
in a ceaseless shower. All around, the life-giving earth roared
as it burned, and vast forests crackled loudly in the fire.
All the land boiled, and so did the streams of Oceanus
and the barren sea. Hot vapor wrapped around
the Titans beneath the earth, and flame reached the bright upper air,
boundless flame. Their eyes were blinded, strong as they were,
by the dazzling glare of thunderbolt and lightning.
An astonishing heat filled Chaos, the great chasm. To see it before you
with your own eyes and hear the sound with your own ears
was just as though Gaia, the Earth, and wide Ouranos, the Sky above,
were crashing together. Such a mighty roar would rise
if Earth were collapsing and Sky came crashing down from high above.
So great was the crash as the gods met in battle.
The winds roared amid the shaking and dust,
the thunder and lightning and smoking thunderbolts,
the weapons of great Zeus, and carried cries and shouts
between the two armies. An immense uproar rose
from that dreadful conflict, and their deeds revealed their strength.

notes.label: Zeus
notes.general: The god who commands thunder and lightning.
notes.here: He releases his full power against the Titans.

notes.label: Olympus
notes.general: A high mountain associated with the home of the gods.
notes.here: Zeus advances from heaven and Olympus as he attacks.

notes.label: Thunderbolt
notes.general: A bolt of lightning imagined as a weapon a god can throw.
notes.here: Zeus hurls thunderbolts wrapped in sacred flame.

notes.label: Oceanus
notes.general: The great river believed to circle the world, and the god of that river.
notes.here: Even its waters boil under Zeus’s fire.

notes.label: Barren sea
notes.general: A poetic description of the sea as producing no crops.
notes.here: It does not mean the sea has no living creatures.

notes.label: Titans
notes.general: An older generation of gods.
notes.here: Zeus’s enemies are surrounded by hot vapor and blinded by lightning.

notes.label: Chaos
notes.general: The vast opening or gulf that appears at the beginning of Hesiod’s universe.
notes.here: The name means a yawning gap, rather than everyday confusion. Zeus’s heat fills it.

notes.label: Gaia
notes.general: Earth herself, understood as a goddess.
notes.here: The battle sounds as though she were collapsing beneath a falling Sky.

notes.label: Ouranos
notes.general: Sky himself, understood as a god.
notes.here: Hesiod imagines how it would sound if he crashed down onto Gaia.

passages.title: The Titans are defeated
passages.summary: Three mighty fighters defeat the Titans and imprison them in Tartarus, far below the earth.

verses.text: Then the battle turned; until then, both sides had held their ground,
fighting steadfastly through the fierce clashes.
At the front, Cottus, Briareus, and Gyges stirred up savage battle,
warriors who could never have their fill of war.
From their powerful hands they hurled three hundred rocks
in quick succession, overshadowing with their missiles
the Titans, whom they sent beneath the earth with its wide roads
and bound in painful chains,
overpowering them with their hands, proud though the Titans were,
as far beneath the earth as the sky is above it.
That is how far it is from earth to misty Tartarus.
For nine nights and nine days a bronze anvil
falling from the sky would reach the earth on the tenth day;
and again, for nine nights and nine days a bronze anvil
falling from earth would reach Tartarus on the tenth.
A bronze fence surrounds Tartarus, and Night
spreads in three layers around its neck, while above it
grow the roots of earth and the sea that yields no harvest.

notes.label: Cottus, Briareus, and Gyges
notes.general: Three giant brothers, each with a hundred hands.
notes.here: Their many hands let them throw three hundred rocks at once.

notes.label: Titans
notes.general: An older generation of gods.
notes.here: They lose the war against Zeus and his allies.

notes.label: Tartarus
notes.general: A dark region far beneath the earth.
notes.here: It becomes the Titans’ prison.

notes.label: Bronze anvil
notes.general: An anvil is a heavy metal block used when hammering metal into shape. Bronze is a metal made mainly from copper and tin.
notes.here: Even this heavy object would take ten days to fall to Tartarus.

notes.label: Roots of earth and sea
notes.general: Hesiod imagines earth and sea as having roots extending into the depths.
notes.here: These roots grow above Tartarus.

notes.label: The sea that yields no harvest
notes.general: A poetic description of the sea, where crops cannot grow.
notes.here: It contrasts the sea with cultivated land.

passages.title: Deep Tartarus
passages.summary: The Titans cannot escape. Around their prison lie terrifying depths that even the gods fear.

verses.text: There the Titan gods lie hidden in misty darkness,
by the will of Zeus, the cloud-gatherer,
in a dank place at the ends of the vast earth.
They cannot get out. Poseidon has fitted doors
of bronze across the entrance, and a wall runs around on either side.
There Gyges, Cottus, and great-hearted Obriareus
live as faithful guards of Zeus, who carries the aegis.
There, of dark earth and misty Tartarus,
of the sea that yields no harvest and the starry sky,
the sources and boundaries all lie side by side,
dreadful, dank places that even the gods hate.
There is a huge chasm: even in a whole year
you would not reach its floor, once you had passed inside its gates.
Instead, storm after storm would carry you this way and that,
savage storms. Even the immortal gods find terrifying
this marvel. There stands the fearsome house of dark Night,

notes.label: Zeus
notes.general: The ruler of the gods, associated with the sky, storms, and thunder.
notes.here: He orders the Titans’ imprisonment and appoints their guards.

notes.label: Poseidon
notes.general: The god of the sea and earthquakes.
notes.here: He installs the bronze doors that shut the Titans in.

notes.label: Obriareus
notes.general: Another form of the name Briareus.
notes.here: He guards the Titans with his brothers Gyges and Cottus.

notes.label: Aegis
notes.general: A divine protective object, often described as a shield or animal skin.
notes.here: Carrying it is one of Zeus’s identifying features.

notes.label: Dank
notes.general: Unpleasantly damp and cold.
notes.here: It describes the gloomy depths beneath the earth.

notes.label: Chasm
notes.general: A huge, deep opening.
notes.here: Storms toss anyone inside it about for longer than a year.

notes.label: Night
notes.general: Night is a goddess as well as the darkness that comes each evening.
notes.here: Her house stands near these terrifying depths.

passages.title: Night, Day, Sleep, and Death
passages.summary: Night and Day take turns travelling over the earth. Sleep is gentle, but Death never releases anyone he catches.

verses.text: wrapped in blue-black clouds.
Before it, Iapetus's son holds up the broad sky,
standing with his head and tireless hands supporting it,
unshaken. Here Night and Day draw near
and greet each other as they cross the great threshold
of bronze. One goes inside while the other
goes out; the house never holds them both at once.
One is always outside the house,
travelling over the earth, while the other stays inside
and waits until her own time to set out arrives.
Day brings people on earth the light that lets them see far,
while Night holds Sleep in her hands, the brother of Death,
deadly Night, wrapped in a misty cloud.
There the children of dark Night have their homes,
Sleep and Death, fearsome gods. Never does
shining Helios, the Sun, look upon them with his rays,
either as he climbs into the sky or as he comes down from it.
Sleep travels over the earth and the broad back of the sea,
peaceful and gentle toward human beings.
But Death has a heart of iron, and a heart of bronze
lies merciless within his chest; he holds on to whoever he first seizes
among humankind. Even the immortal gods hate him.

notes.label: Iapetus’s son
notes.general: Atlas, a son of the Titan Iapetus.
notes.here: He holds up the sky with his head and hands.

notes.label: Day
notes.general: Day is a goddess as well as the daylight hours.
notes.here: She and Night share a house but are never inside together.

notes.label: Threshold
notes.general: The strip across the bottom of a doorway.
notes.here: Night and Day pass each other at the bronze entrance.

notes.label: Sleep
notes.general: The god of sleep, a son of Night and brother of Death.
notes.here: He moves gently among human beings.

notes.label: Death
notes.general: The god who personifies death, another son of Night.
notes.here: His iron and bronze heart expresses his lack of mercy.

notes.label: Helios
notes.general: The Sun, imagined as a god travelling across the sky.
notes.here: His rays never reach Sleep and Death.

notes.label: Immortal
notes.general: Unable to die.
notes.here: Even gods who cannot die hate Death.

passages.title: The guard at the gate
passages.summary: The dog welcomes people into the home of Hades and Persephone, but eats anyone he catches leaving.

verses.text: There, in front, stand the echoing halls of the god below,
mighty Hades, and of dreaded Persephone.
A fearsome dog keeps watch before them,
merciless, with a cruel trick: as people enter,
he greets them all with wagging tail and both ears,
but never lets them back out. Instead, he lies in wait
and devours anyone he catches going outside the gates
of mighty Hades and dreaded Persephone.

notes.label: Hades
notes.general: The god who rules the world of the dead.
notes.here: His halls stand in the depths, guarded by a dog.

notes.label: Persephone
notes.general: The queen of the dead, who rules alongside Hades.
notes.here: She shares the echoing halls.

notes.label: The guard dog
notes.general: Cerberus, the dog guarding the world of the dead.
notes.here: Hesiod does not name him in these lines. His friendly welcome hides a deadly trap.

passages.title: The oath by Styx
passages.summary: The gods swear their strongest oath by the water of Styx. A god who breaks it lies helpless for a year, then spends nine years apart from the other gods.

verses.text: There lives a goddess hated by the immortals,
dread Styx, daughter of Oceanus, the river that flows back on itself,
his eldest child. Far from the gods she lives in a splendid house,
sheltered by towering rocks, and all around
silver pillars hold it up toward the sky.
Rarely does swift-footed Iris, daughter of Thaumas,
come across the sea’s broad back with a message.
But whenever quarrels and strife arise among the immortals,
and one of the gods who live on Olympus tells a lie,
Zeus sends Iris to fetch the gods’ great oath,
the famous water, brought from far away in a golden jug,
cold water that trickles down from a sheer rock
high above. Far beneath the earth with its broad roads,
a branch of the sacred river flows through black night,
a branch of Oceanus, with a tenth of his water set apart.
The other nine parts wind around the earth and the sea’s broad back
in silver swirls, then pour into the sea.
That one part flows from the rock, a great source of pain for the gods.
Whoever pours out this water and swears a false oath over it,
among the immortals who dwell on snowy Olympus’ summit,
lies breathless for a full year.
They never come near ambrosia or nectar
to take nourishment, but lie without breath or speech
on a bed spread for them, wrapped in a dreadful coma.
When that sickness has lasted a full year,
another, harsher ordeal follows in its turn.
For nine years they are cut off from the gods who live forever,
never joining their councils or their feasts
for all those nine years. In the tenth they join once more
the gatherings of the immortals who live on Olympus.
Such is the oath the gods established, the unfailing water of Styx,
ancient water that flows through a harsh and rocky place.

notes.label: Styx
notes.general: A goddess and an underworld river. Her water makes the gods’ most binding oath.
notes.here: She lives apart from the other gods, who face severe punishment if they swear falsely by her water.

notes.label: Oceanus
notes.general: The divine river imagined as flowing around the world.
notes.here: He is Styx’s father, and her stream receives one tenth of his water.

notes.label: Iris
notes.general: A swift messenger of the gods, associated with the rainbow.
notes.here: Zeus sends her to fetch the water of Styx in a golden jug.

notes.label: Thaumas
notes.general: A sea god and the father of Iris.
notes.here: Hesiod identifies Iris by naming her father.

notes.label: Zeus
notes.general: The ruler of the gods, whose weapon is the thunderbolt.
notes.here: He sends for the water when a dispute involves a god’s lie.

notes.label: Olympus
notes.general: The mountain where Zeus and the other ruling gods have their homes.
notes.here: A punished god is excluded from their councils and feasts.

notes.label: Ambrosia and nectar
notes.general: The gods’ food and drink.
notes.here: A god who swears falsely cannot eat or drink them during the year of helplessness.

notes.label: Coma
notes.general: A deep state of unconsciousness in which someone cannot wake or respond.
notes.here: The offending god lies unable to breathe or speak for a full year.

passages.title: At the world's limits
passages.summary: At the world’s dark limits stand great gates. The Titans live beyond them, while Zeus’s allies have homes near Oceanus. Briareus marries Poseidon’s daughter.

verses.text: There, dark earth and misty Tartarus,
the barren sea and the starry sky
all have their sources and their limits side by side,
grim, moldy places that even the gods hate.
There stand gleaming gates and a bronze threshold,
unshakable, fixed on roots that stretch unbroken below,
grown there of itself. In front, apart from all the gods,
the Titans live beyond gloomy Chaos.
The famous allies of loudly thundering Zeus
live in homes at the foundations of Oceanus,
Cottus and Gyes. As for noble Briareus,
Poseidon, the Earth-shaker whose crashes thunder deep, made him his son-in-law,
giving him his daughter Cymopolea to marry.

notes.label: Tartarus
notes.general: A vast, dark region far beneath the earth.
notes.here: Its sources and limits lie beside those of earth, sea and sky.

notes.label: Chaos
notes.general: The primordial gap or chasm; the name does not simply mean disorder.
notes.here: The Titans live on the far side of this gloomy gulf.

notes.label: Titans
notes.general: An older generation of gods defeated by Zeus and his allies.
notes.here: They live confined beyond the gates, apart from the other gods.

notes.label: Threshold
notes.general: The sill across the bottom of a doorway.
notes.here: This bronze threshold is firmly rooted in the depths.

notes.label: Cottus and Gyes
notes.general: Two of three giant brothers, each with a hundred hands and fifty heads.
notes.here: They helped Zeus defeat the Titans and now live at Oceanus’s foundations.

notes.label: Briareus
notes.general: The third of the hundred-handed brothers who helped Zeus.
notes.here: Poseidon makes him his son-in-law by giving him Cymopolea in marriage.

notes.label: Poseidon, the Earth-shaker
notes.general: The god of the sea and earthquakes. “Earth-shaker” is one of his titles.
notes.here: The Greek names him by his title; he is Cymopolea’s father.

notes.label: Cymopolea
notes.general: A divine daughter of Poseidon.
notes.here: She becomes Briareus’s wife.

notes.label: Oceanus
notes.general: The divine river that circles the world.
notes.here: Cottus and Gyes have their homes at his foundations.

notes.label: Zeus
notes.general: The ruler of the gods, associated with thunder and lightning.
notes.here: Cottus, Gyes and Briareus were his allies against the Titans.

passages.title: Earth bears Typhoeus
passages.summary: Gaia and Tartarus have a terrifying child, Typhoeus. With a hundred fiery snake heads and many strange voices, he nearly becomes ruler of gods and humans.

verses.text: After Zeus had driven the Titans out of heaven,
vast Gaia gave birth to her youngest child, Typhoeus,
joining in love with Tartarus through golden Aphrodite.
Typhoeus had hands of strength, ready for mighty deeds,
and tireless feet, a powerful god. From his shoulders
grew a hundred snake heads, the heads of a terrifying serpent,
flicking their dark tongues. From his eyes,
beneath the brows of those monstrous heads, fire flashed;
from every head fire blazed as he stared.
Voices sounded in all his fearsome heads,
sending out every kind of astonishing cry. Sometimes
they spoke so that the gods could understand; at other times
they gave the voice of a proud, bellowing bull with unstoppable force,
or of a lion with a ruthless heart;
sometimes they sounded like puppies, a wonder to hear;
sometimes he hissed, and the tall mountains echoed.
That day a disaster beyond all help would have happened,
and Typhoeus would have ruled over mortals and immortals,
if Zeus, the father of gods and humans, had not been quick to notice.

notes.label: Gaia
notes.general: Earth herself, understood as a goddess.
notes.here: She gives birth to Typhoeus, her youngest child.

notes.label: Tartarus
notes.general: Both the deep region beneath the earth and a divine being.
notes.here: He is Typhoeus’s father.

notes.label: Typhoeus
notes.general: A monstrous divine being who challenges Zeus for rule.
notes.here: He has a hundred snake heads, blazing eyes and voices that imitate many creatures.

notes.label: Aphrodite
notes.general: The goddess of love and sexual desire, often called “golden.”
notes.here: Her power brings Gaia and Tartarus together.

notes.label: Zeus
notes.general: The ruler of the gods, called the father of gods and humans.
notes.here: He notices the threat before Typhoeus can take control.

notes.label: Titans
notes.general: The older gods whom Zeus defeated in a war for power.
notes.here: Their defeat comes before Typhoeus’s birth.

notes.label: Mortals and immortals
notes.general: Humans, who die, and gods, who live forever.
notes.here: Typhoeus nearly gains power over both.

passages.title: Zeus defeats Typhoeus
passages.summary: Zeus defeats Typhoeus with his thunderbolt. Their battle shakes and burns the world, and Zeus throws the monster into Tartarus.

verses.text: Zeus thundered with a harsh and mighty crash, and all around the earth
rang terribly, as did the wide sky above,
the sea, the streams of Oceanus, and Tartarus beneath the earth.
Great Olympus shook beneath the immortal feet
of the king as he sprang into action, and the earth groaned.
Heat from both fighters gripped the violet-dark sea,
from thunder and lightning, from the monster's fire,
from fiery blasts of wind and the blazing thunderbolt.
All the earth boiled, and the sky and sea.
Long waves raged around the shores on every side
under the force of the immortals, and the shaking would not stop.
Hades trembled, ruler of the dead below,
and so did the Titans deep in Tartarus, gathered around Cronus,
at the endless roar and the terrible fighting.
Then Zeus gathered all his strength and took up his weapons,
thunder, lightning, and the smoking thunderbolt.
He leaped from Olympus and struck, scorching all
the monstrous heads of the terrifying creature.
When Zeus had beaten him down with blow after blow,
Typhoeus fell, his limbs powerless, and the vast earth groaned.
Flame rushed from the thunderstruck lord Typhoeus
in the mountain's dark and rugged valleys,
as he lay stricken. A great stretch of the vast earth burned
in the tremendous heat and melted like tin
heated by skilled young men in well-pierced crucibles,
or like iron, the strongest metal of all,
which yields to blazing fire in mountain valleys
and melts in the sacred earth beneath Hephaestus's hands.
So the earth melted in the glare of the burning fire.
In bitter anger, Zeus hurled Typhoeus into wide Tartarus.

notes.label: Zeus
notes.general: The god of the sky and thunder, who becomes ruler of the gods.
notes.here: He uses thunder, lightning, and his thunderbolt against Typhoeus.

notes.label: Typhoeus
notes.general: A gigantic monster with many snake heads, also called Typhon.
notes.here: He fights Zeus with fire and is defeated.

notes.label: Oceanus
notes.general: A divine river believed to flow around the world.
notes.here: His streams shake with the rest of the world.

notes.label: Olympus
notes.general: The mountain where Zeus and the other Olympian gods have their home.
notes.here: It shakes beneath Zeus’s feet before he leaps into battle.

notes.label: Tartarus
notes.general: A deep, dark place far beneath the earth.
notes.here: The defeated Titans are there, and Zeus throws Typhoeus there too.

notes.label: Hades
notes.general: The god who rules the world of the dead.
notes.here: Even he trembles at the battle.

notes.label: Titans and Cronus
notes.general: The Titans are an older generation of gods. Cronus, Zeus’s father, was their ruler.
notes.here: They tremble together in Tartarus, where they are held after their defeat.

notes.label: Hephaestus
notes.general: The god of metalworking and the forge.
notes.here: His melting of iron shows how the battle’s heat melts the earth.

notes.label: Crucible
notes.general: A container that can withstand the heat needed to melt metal.
notes.here: The earth melts as tin does in a metalworker’s crucible.

passages.title: Storm winds and Zeus's rule
passages.summary: Typhoeus is the source of destructive storm winds. After defeating the Titans, the gods choose Zeus as king, and he gives them their honors.

verses.text: From Typhoeus comes the force of the moisture-laden winds,
except for Notus, Boreas, and sky-clearing Zephyrus.
These are born of the gods, a great help to mortals,
but the others blow across the sea as reckless gusts.
They fall upon the misty sea
and rage in vicious storms, bringing great suffering to mortals.
Now one wind blows, now another; they scatter ships
and kill sailors. There is no defense against this harm
for people who meet these winds at sea.
These winds also sweep across the boundless, flowering earth
and ruin the lovely work of earth-born people,
filling the land with dust and a dreadful uproar.
When the blessed gods had brought their struggle to an end
and settled by force their dispute with the Titans over honors,
they urged Zeus to be king and ruler,
the far-seeing god of Olympus, on Gaia's advice,
to reign over the immortals. Zeus shared out their honors among them.

notes.label: Typhoeus
notes.general: The monstrous enemy Zeus has just defeated.
notes.here: Hesiod makes him the source of dangerous winds.

notes.label: Notus
notes.general: The South Wind, imagined as a god.
notes.here: Hesiod groups him with the winds that help people.

notes.label: Boreas
notes.general: The North Wind, imagined as a god.
notes.here: He is one of the three winds distinguished from Typhoeus’s destructive gusts.

notes.label: Zephyrus
notes.general: The West Wind, imagined as a god.
notes.here: He is described as clearing the sky.

notes.label: Gaia
notes.general: Earth herself, understood as a goddess.
notes.here: She advises the gods to make Zeus their king.

notes.label: Titans
notes.general: An older generation of gods who fought Zeus and his allies.
notes.here: Their defeat settles which gods will hold power.

notes.label: Olympian Zeus
notes.general: Zeus is the god of thunder. “Olympian” connects him with Mount Olympus, the gods’ home.
notes.here: The gods choose him to rule them.

notes.label: Honors
notes.general: A god’s recognized rank, privileges, and share of power.
notes.here: Zeus assigns each god a place in the new order.

passages.title: Zeus and Metis
passages.summary: Zeus swallows his wise wife Metis because her future son is destined to replace him as king. Inside Zeus, she can advise him.

verses.text: Zeus, king of the gods, made Metis his first wife.
She knew more than any other god or mortal.
But when Metis was about to give birth to bright-eyed Athena,
Zeus cunningly deceived her mind
with coaxing words and swallowed her into his belly,
on the advice of Gaia and starry Uranus.
They had advised him to do this so that no one else
would hold Zeus's royal place among the everlasting gods.
For Metis was destined to bear children of great wisdom:
first a daughter, bright-eyed Athena, called Tritogeneia,
equal to her father in strength and wise judgment.
Then Metis was to bear a son, a king of gods and humans,
with a fierce and mighty heart.
But before that, Zeus swallowed Metis into his belly,
so that the goddess could advise him on good and evil.

notes.label: Zeus
notes.general: The king of the gods.
notes.here: He swallows Metis to prevent the birth of a son who would take his throne.

notes.label: Metis
notes.general: A goddess whose name means cleverness or wise planning.
notes.here: She is Zeus’s first wife, Athena’s mother, and a source of advice.

notes.label: Athena / Tritogeneia
notes.general: Athena is a goddess of wisdom, warfare, and skilled crafts. Tritogeneia is another name for her.
notes.here: Metis’s first child will match Zeus in strength and wise judgment.

notes.label: Gaia
notes.general: Earth herself, understood as a goddess.
notes.here: She helps Zeus protect his rule by advising him to swallow Metis.

notes.label: Uranus
notes.general: Sky himself, understood as a god and Gaia’s partner.
notes.here: He joins Gaia in advising Zeus.

passages.title: Zeus's divine children
passages.summary: Zeus has children with several goddesses. Their children include the Seasons, the Fates, the Graces, Persephone, and the nine Muses.

verses.text: Next Zeus married radiant Themis, who bore the Seasons,
Eunomia, Dike, and flourishing Eirene,
who watch over the work of mortal people,
and the Fates, whom Zeus the wise planner honored above all:
Clotho, Lachesis, and Atropos, who give
mortal people their share of good and bad.
Eurynome bore Zeus three Graces with beautiful cheeks,
a daughter of Oceanus, lovely to look upon:
Aglaia, Euphrosyne, and lovely Thalia.
From their eyes as they gazed, desire flowed,
melting the limbs; beautiful were their glances beneath their brows.
Then Zeus came to the bed of Demeter, who feeds so many.
She bore white-armed Persephone, whom Aidoneus
snatched from her mother; Zeus the wise planner gave her to him.
Then Zeus fell in love with lovely-haired Mnemosyne,
who bore him the Muses with golden headbands,
nine daughters who delight in feasts and the joy of song.

notes.label: Zeus
notes.general: King of the gods.
notes.here: He fathers the children listed in this section and gives Persephone to Aidoneus.

notes.label: Themis
notes.general: A goddess of divine order and what is right.
notes.here: Zeus's second wife and the mother of the Seasons and the Fates.

notes.label: The Seasons
notes.general: The Horae: goddesses who oversee the seasons and orderly life.
notes.here: Eunomia means Good Order, Dike means Justice, and Eirene means Peace. They watch over human work.

notes.label: The Fates
notes.general: Goddesses who determine people's allotted lives.
notes.here: Clotho, Lachesis, and Atropos give people their share of good and bad. Their names suggest spinning, allotting, and what cannot be turned back.

notes.label: Eurynome
notes.general: A goddess and daughter of Oceanus.
notes.here: She and Zeus are the parents of the three Graces.

notes.label: Oceanus
notes.general: The divine river believed to flow around the world.
notes.here: He is Eurynome's father.

notes.label: The Graces
notes.general: Goddesses of beauty, charm, and delight.
notes.here: Aglaia, Euphrosyne, and Thalia have names suggesting splendor, good cheer, and flourishing.

notes.label: Demeter
notes.general: Goddess of grain and farming.
notes.here: She feeds many through the earth's crops and is Persephone's mother.

notes.label: Persephone
notes.general: Daughter of Demeter and Zeus, and queen of the underworld.
notes.here: Aidoneus takes her away from her mother with Zeus's agreement.

notes.label: Aidoneus
notes.general: Another name for Hades, ruler of the underworld.
notes.here: He snatches Persephone away.

notes.label: Mnemosyne
notes.general: The goddess of memory.
notes.here: She and Zeus are the parents of the nine Muses.

notes.label: The Muses
notes.general: Nine goddesses who inspire song, poetry, and other arts.
notes.here: They wear golden headbands and delight in feasting and singing.

passages.title: Leto, Hera, Athena, and Hephaestus
passages.summary: Leto and Hera bear children to Zeus. Zeus brings Athena from his head, and Hera gives birth to Hephaestus on her own.

verses.text: Leto bore Apollo and Artemis the archer,
children lovelier than all the other gods of heaven,
after joining in love with Zeus, who bears the aegis.
Last of all, Zeus made Hera in her full bloom his wife.
She bore Hebe, Ares, and Eileithyia,
joining in love with the king of gods and humans.
Zeus himself brought forth bright-eyed Athena, called Tritogeneia, from his head,
fearsome and tireless, stirring up battle and leading armies,
a mighty goddess who delights in the clash of fighting, in wars and battles.
Hera, without joining anyone in love, bore famous Hephaestus,
furious with her husband and quarreling with him.
He surpassed all the gods of heaven in craftsmanship.

notes.label: Leto
notes.general: A goddess and the mother of Apollo and Artemis.
notes.here: She bears these two children after joining Zeus in love.

notes.label: Apollo
notes.general: A god associated with archery, music, healing, and prophecy.
notes.here: The son of Leto and Zeus.

notes.label: Artemis
notes.general: Goddess of hunting and wild animals.
notes.here: Leto and Zeus's daughter, described as an archer.

notes.label: Aegis
notes.general: A divine protective object, described as a shield or a skin worn or carried.
notes.here: Bearing it is one of Zeus's marks of power.

notes.label: Hera
notes.general: Queen of the gods and a goddess of marriage.
notes.here: Zeus's last wife in this account. She also gives birth to Hephaestus without a partner.

notes.label: Hebe
notes.general: The goddess of youth.
notes.here: A daughter of Hera and Zeus.

notes.label: Ares
notes.general: A god of war.
notes.here: A son of Hera and Zeus.

notes.label: Eileithyia
notes.general: A goddess who helps women in childbirth.
notes.here: A daughter of Hera and Zeus.

notes.label: Athena / Tritogeneia
notes.general: Athena is a goddess of wisdom, warfare, and skilled work. Tritogeneia is one of her traditional titles.
notes.here: She emerges from Zeus's head as a fearsome leader in battle. Atrytone, another title in the Greek, is translated as “tireless.”

notes.label: Hephaestus
notes.general: The god of fire and craftsmanship, especially metalworking.
notes.here: Hera bears him on her own. His skill exceeds that of every other god.

passages.title: Poseidon, Ares, and Zeus
passages.summary: Hesiod names more divine parents and children, including Triton, Hermes, Dionysus, and Heracles. He also names the wives of Cadmus and Hephaestus.

verses.text: From Amphitrite and the thundering Earth-shaker Poseidon
came great Triton, mighty in strength, who lives
at the bottom of the sea, beside his dear mother and his father the king,
in a golden house, a fearsome god. And to Ares,
the shield-piercer, Cytherea bore Phobos and Deimos,
terrifying sons who throw tightly packed ranks of warriors into confusion
in chilling war, alongside Ares the city-sacker.
She also bore Harmonia, whom bold Cadmus made his wife.
Maia, daughter of Atlas, bore glorious Hermes to Zeus,
the immortals' messenger, after entering Zeus's sacred bed.
Semele, daughter of Cadmus, bore Zeus a splendid son
after joining him in love: Dionysus, full of joy.
She was mortal, her son immortal; now both are gods.
Alcmene gave birth to mighty Heracles
after joining in love with Zeus the cloud-gatherer.
Hephaestus, the renowned god with disabled legs, made Aglaia,
the youngest of the Graces, his wife in her full bloom.

notes.label: Amphitrite
notes.general: A sea goddess and Poseidon's wife.
notes.here: Triton's mother, who lives with him and Poseidon beneath the sea.

notes.label: Poseidon / Earth-shaker
notes.general: God of the sea and earthquakes.
notes.here: “Earth-shaker” translates Ennosigaios, his title in the Greek. He is Triton's father.

notes.label: Triton
notes.general: A sea god, son of Amphitrite and Poseidon.
notes.here: He lives with his parents in a golden house on the sea floor.

notes.label: Cytherea
notes.general: A title of Aphrodite, goddess of love, linked to the island of Cythera.
notes.here: She and Ares are the parents of Phobos, Deimos, and Harmonia.

notes.label: Ares
notes.general: A god of war.
notes.here: He pierces shields and destroys cities; Phobos and Deimos join him in battle.

notes.label: Phobos and Deimos
notes.general: Divine figures whose names mean Panic and Terror.
notes.here: These sons of Ares and Cytherea scatter the ordered ranks of soldiers.

notes.label: Harmonia
notes.general: A goddess whose name means Harmony.
notes.here: The daughter of Ares and Cytherea, and the wife of Cadmus.

notes.label: Cadmus
notes.general: A legendary founder of the Greek city of Thebes.
notes.here: Harmonia's husband and Semele's father.

notes.label: Maia and Atlas
notes.general: Maia is a goddess. Her father Atlas holds up the sky.
notes.here: Maia bears Hermes to Zeus.

notes.label: Hermes
notes.general: Messenger of the gods.
notes.here: The son of Maia and Zeus.

notes.label: Semele
notes.general: A mortal daughter of Cadmus and the mother of Dionysus.
notes.here: Hesiod says that she has now become a goddess.

notes.label: Dionysus
notes.general: God of wine and festive celebration.
notes.here: The joyful, immortal son of Zeus and the once-mortal Semele.

notes.label: Alcmene and Heracles
notes.general: Alcmene is a mortal woman. Her son Heracles is a hero famous for his strength.
notes.here: Zeus is Heracles' father.

notes.label: Hephaestus and Aglaia
notes.general: Hephaestus is the god of craftsmanship. Aglaia is one of the three Graces.
notes.here: He marries Aglaia, the youngest Grace.

passages.title: Dionysus, Heracles, and more
passages.summary: Ariadne becomes immortal, and Heracles marries Hebe and lives safely among the gods. Hesiod then traces the family of Helios down to Medea.

verses.text: Golden-haired Dionysus made fair-haired Ariadne,
daughter of Minos, his wife in her full bloom.
For his sake, Zeus son of Cronus made her immortal and free from aging.
The brave son of Alcmene of the lovely ankles took Hebe,
mighty Heracles, after completing his painful labors,
the daughter of great Zeus and Hera of the golden sandals,
as his honored wife on snowy Olympus.
Happy Heracles! His great work accomplished, he lives among the immortals,
free from harm and aging for all time.
To tireless Helios, the renowned daughter of Oceanus,
Perseis, bore Circe and King Aeetes.
Aeetes, son of Helios who shines on mortals,
married a daughter of Oceanus, the river that circles the world,
beautiful-cheeked Idyia, in keeping with the gods' wishes.
Idyia bore him Medea of the lovely ankles,
yielding to him in love through golden Aphrodite's power.

notes.label: Dionysus
notes.general: God of wine and festive celebration.
notes.here: He marries Ariadne, whom Zeus makes immortal for his sake.

notes.label: Ariadne and Minos
notes.general: Ariadne is a daughter of Minos, a legendary king of Crete.
notes.here: She becomes Dionysus's wife and receives freedom from death and aging.

notes.label: Zeus / son of Cronus
notes.general: Zeus is king of the gods. Cronus is his father.
notes.here: “Son of Cronus” translates the title Cronion. Zeus makes Ariadne immortal.

notes.label: Heracles and Alcmene
notes.general: Heracles is the strong hero born to Alcmene and Zeus.
notes.here: After his painful labors, he marries Hebe and lives forever among the gods.

notes.label: Labors
notes.general: Difficult tasks that demand great effort.
notes.here: The dangerous feats Heracles had to complete. These lines do not list them.

notes.label: Hebe and Hera
notes.general: Hebe is the goddess of youth. Hera is queen of the gods.
notes.here: Hebe, daughter of Zeus and Hera, marries Heracles.

notes.label: Olympus
notes.general: The mountain that is home to the gods.
notes.here: Heracles marries Hebe on its snowy heights.

notes.label: Perseis
notes.general: A divine daughter of Oceanus.
notes.here: She and Helios are the parents of Circe and Aeetes.

notes.label: Helios
notes.general: The Sun, understood as a god.
notes.here: Called tireless because of his continuing journey across the sky.

notes.label: Circe
notes.general: A goddess known for her magical powers.
notes.here: Daughter of Helios and Perseis, and sister of Aeetes.

notes.label: Aeetes
notes.general: A legendary king of Colchis, on the Black Sea.
notes.here: Son of Helios and Perseis, husband of Idyia, and father of Medea.

notes.label: Oceanus and Idyia
notes.general: Oceanus is the divine river surrounding the world. Idyia is one of his daughters.
notes.here: Idyia marries Aeetes with the gods' agreement.

notes.label: Medea
notes.general: A woman famous in Greek myth for her magical knowledge.
notes.here: The daughter of Aeetes and Idyia.

notes.label: Aphrodite
notes.general: Goddess of love and sexual desire.
notes.here: Her power brings Idyia and Aeetes together in love. “Golden” is a traditional description of her.

passages.title: A new song begins
passages.summary: The poet asks the Muses to sing about goddesses who had children with mortal men.

verses.text: Now farewell, you who live in the halls of Olympus,
and you islands and mainlands, and the salt sea between them.
Now sing of the family of goddesses, sweet-voiced
Muses of Olympus, daughters of Zeus who carries the aegis,
all those who slept beside mortal men
and, though immortal, bore children like gods.

notes.label: Olympus
notes.general: The mountain where the gods have their home.
notes.here: The poet says farewell to the gods before starting a new subject.

notes.label: Muses
notes.general: Goddesses of song and poetry, and daughters of Zeus.
notes.here: The poet asks them to tell the next part of his song.

notes.label: Zeus
notes.general: King of the gods.
notes.here: He is named as the Muses’ father.

notes.label: Aegis
notes.general: A powerful divine shield or protective covering associated with Zeus.
notes.here: Carrying the aegis is a sign of Zeus’s power.

notes.label: Mortal and immortal
notes.general: Mortals can die; immortals live forever.
notes.here: The mothers are goddesses, while the fathers are mortal men.

passages.title: Goddesses and mortal families
passages.summary: Several goddesses have children with mortal men. Their children include the bringer of wealth, royal families, and mighty heroes.

verses.text: Demeter, radiant among goddesses, bore Plutus
after joining the hero Iasion in sweet love
in a field plowed three times, in the fertile land of Crete,
kindly Plutus, who travels over the earth and the sea’s broad back,
everywhere. Whoever meets him, whoever’s hands he comes into,
he makes rich and grants great wealth.
Harmonia, daughter of golden Aphrodite, bore Cadmus
Ino and Semele and lovely-cheeked Agave,
and Autonoe, whom Aristaeus with his thick hair married,
and Polydorus, in Thebes with its beautiful crown.
Callirhoe, daughter of Oceanus, joined strong-hearted Chrysaor
in love through Aphrodite, rich in gold,
and bore a son, the strongest of all mortals,
Geryon, whom mighty Heracles killed
for his cattle with their rolling gait, on Erytheia, surrounded by the sea.
Eos bore Tithonus Memnon in his bronze helmet,
king of the Ethiopians, and lord Emathion.
With Cephalus, Eos brought forth a glorious son,
mighty Phaethon, a man like the gods.

notes.label: Demeter
notes.general: Goddess of grain and farming.
notes.here: She has Plutus with Iasion in a plowed field.

notes.label: Iasion
notes.general: A mortal hero who becomes Demeter’s lover.
notes.here: He is Plutus’s father.

notes.label: Crete
notes.general: A large Greek island.
notes.here: Its fertile farmland is the setting for Demeter and Iasion’s love.

notes.label: Plutus
notes.general: The god of wealth; his name means “wealth.”
notes.here: He brings riches to anyone he reaches.

notes.label: Harmonia
notes.general: A goddess whose name means “harmony.”
notes.here: Aphrodite’s daughter and Cadmus’s partner.

notes.label: Aphrodite
notes.general: Goddess of love and sexual desire.
notes.here: She is Harmonia’s mother, and her power brings Callirhoe and Chrysaor together.

notes.label: Cadmus
notes.general: The legendary founder of Thebes.
notes.here: He has five children with Harmonia.

notes.label: Thebes
notes.general: An important city in ancient Greece.
notes.here: Its “beautiful crown” may suggest the walls or towers around it.

notes.label: Ino
notes.general: A daughter of Cadmus and Harmonia.
notes.here: The first of their children named in this list.

notes.label: Semele
notes.general: A daughter of Cadmus and Harmonia, and mother of the god Dionysus.
notes.here: She appears among the children born at Thebes.

notes.label: Agave
notes.general: A daughter of Cadmus and Harmonia.
notes.here: The poem describes her lovely cheeks.

notes.label: Autonoe
notes.general: A daughter of Cadmus and Harmonia.
notes.here: She marries Aristaeus.

notes.label: Aristaeus
notes.general: A divine figure linked with herding, beekeeping, and farming.
notes.here: Autonoe’s husband, described as having thick, flowing hair.

notes.label: Polydorus
notes.general: A son of Cadmus and Harmonia.
notes.here: He completes the list of their children.

notes.label: Callirhoe
notes.general: A daughter of Oceanus.
notes.here: She and Chrysaor are Geryon’s parents.

notes.label: Oceanus
notes.general: The divine river believed to flow around the world.
notes.here: He is Callirhoe’s father.

notes.label: Chrysaor
notes.general: A powerful figure born from Medusa.
notes.here: He is Geryon’s father.

notes.label: Geryon
notes.general: A mighty, three-headed figure who owned cattle.
notes.here: Heracles kills him to take his herd.

notes.label: Heracles
notes.general: A hero famous for his strength and difficult labors.
notes.here: Taking Geryon’s cattle was one of his labors.

notes.label: Erytheia
notes.general: Geryon’s island, imagined far to the west.
notes.here: The sea surrounds the place where Heracles kills him.

notes.label: Eos
notes.general: Goddess of dawn.
notes.here: She has children with Tithonus and Cephalus.

notes.label: Tithonus
notes.general: A mortal prince loved by Eos.
notes.here: Father of Memnon and Emathion.

notes.label: Memnon
notes.general: A warrior king who fought at Troy.
notes.here: Eos and Tithonus’s son, wearing a bronze helmet.

notes.label: Ethiopians
notes.general: A Greek name for distant peoples imagined near the world’s edges.
notes.here: They are Memnon’s people; the name does not map neatly onto modern Ethiopia.

notes.label: Emathion
notes.general: A son of Eos and Tithonus.
notes.here: Memnon’s brother, given the title “lord.”

notes.label: Cephalus
notes.general: A mortal loved by Eos.
notes.here: He is Phaethon’s father.

notes.label: Phaethon
notes.general: His name means “shining.” Different myths use this name for different figures.
notes.here: This Phaethon is the son of Eos and Cephalus, not the familiar son of the Sun who drives its chariot.

passages.title: Phaethon and Medea
passages.summary: Aphrodite takes Phaethon to serve in her temples. Jason brings Medea home, marries her, and has a son whom Chiron raises.

verses.text: While Phaethon was young, in the tender flower of glorious youth,
a boy with a carefree heart, smile-loving Aphrodite
swept him away and, in her most sacred temples,
made him her attendant by night, a glorious divine spirit.
Medea, daughter of King Aeetes, whom Zeus sustained,
was led away by Jason, Aeson’s son, by the will of the gods who live forever,
away from Aeetes, once Jason had finished the painful trials,
the many tasks imposed by the great, overbearing king,
Pelias, violent and reckless, whose deeds were brutal.
After finishing those trials and suffering greatly, Jason reached Iolcus,
bringing the bright-eyed girl aboard his swift ship,
and Jason, Aeson’s son, made her his wife in the bloom of youth.
Medea, joined in love with Jason, shepherd of his people,
bore a son, Medeius, whom Chiron raised in the mountains,
Chiron, son of Philyra. And great Zeus’s plan was fulfilled.

notes.label: Aphrodite
notes.general: Goddess of love and desire.
notes.here: She takes the young Phaethon away and makes him a divine attendant in her temples.

notes.label: Attendant by night
notes.general: Someone who serves or cares for a temple during the night.
notes.here: Phaethon’s exact duties are not explained; the phrase may also suggest intimacy with Aphrodite.

notes.label: Divine spirit
notes.general: A supernatural being or divine power.
notes.here: Phaethon receives divine status after Aphrodite takes him away.

notes.label: Jason
notes.general: The hero who led the Argonauts in search of the Golden Fleece.
notes.here: Called “son of Aeson” in the Greek, he completes Pelias’s trials and marries Medea.

notes.label: Aeson
notes.general: Jason’s father.
notes.here: The poem twice identifies Jason through his father’s name.

notes.label: Medea
notes.general: Aeetes’s daughter, known for her knowledge of magic.
notes.here: She leaves her father with Jason and becomes his wife.

notes.label: Aeetes
notes.general: King of Colchis, where the Golden Fleece was kept.
notes.here: Medea’s father; the poem describes his royal power as supported by Zeus.

notes.label: Pelias
notes.general: A king of Iolcus who sent Jason after the Golden Fleece.
notes.here: He imposes the difficult trials, and the poet strongly condemns his character.

notes.label: Iolcus
notes.general: A Greek city associated with Jason and Pelias.
notes.here: Jason returns there with Medea.

notes.label: Shepherd of his people
notes.general: A poetic title for a leader, comparing his people to a flock in his care.
notes.here: The title describes Jason.

notes.label: Medeius
notes.general: A son of Jason and Medea.
notes.here: Chiron raises him in the mountains.

notes.label: Chiron
notes.general: A wise centaur, part human and part horse, who raised and taught heroes.
notes.here: He brings up Medeius.

notes.label: Philyra
notes.general: Chiron’s mother, a daughter of Oceanus.
notes.here: The Greek identifies Chiron as her son.

notes.label: Zeus
notes.general: King of the gods.
notes.here: The poet says these events fulfill his plan, without explaining that plan further.

passages.title: Sea goddesses, Circe, and Calypso
passages.summary: More goddesses have children with mortal heroes. Their children include Achilles, Aeneas, and the sons of Odysseus.

verses.text: Then came the daughters of Nereus, the old man of the sea:
Psamathe, radiant among goddesses, bore Phocus
after joining Aeacus in love through golden Aphrodite;
and the silver-footed goddess Thetis joined Peleus
and bore Achilles, who broke through men’s ranks and had a lion’s heart.
Aphrodite, with her beautiful crown, bore Aeneas
after joining the hero Anchises in sweet love
on the heights of wooded Mount Ida with its many folds.
Circe, daughter of Helios, the son of Hyperion,
joined patient-hearted Odysseus in love and bore
Agrius and Latinus, a man both noble and strong.
She also bore Telegonus through golden Aphrodite.
Far, far away, deep among the sacred islands,
they ruled over all the famous Tyrrhenians.
Calypso, radiant among goddesses, bore Odysseus Nausithous
and Nausinous after joining him in sweet love.

notes.label: Nereus
notes.general: An ancient sea god, often called the old man of the sea.
notes.here: Father of Psamathe and Thetis.

notes.label: Psamathe
notes.general: One of Nereus’s daughters, the sea goddesses called Nereids.
notes.here: She has Phocus with Aeacus.

notes.label: Phocus
notes.general: A son of Psamathe and Aeacus.
notes.here: His birth begins this list of sea goddesses’ children.

notes.label: Aeacus
notes.general: A mortal king, and father of Peleus as well as Phocus.
notes.here: He is Psamathe’s partner.

notes.label: Aphrodite / Cytherea
notes.general: Aphrodite is the goddess of love. Cytherea is another name for her, linked to the island of Cythera.
notes.here: She brings Psamathe and Aeacus together, and later bears Aeneas herself.

notes.label: Thetis
notes.general: A sea goddess and daughter of Nereus.
notes.here: Achilles’s mother, described as silver-footed.

notes.label: Peleus
notes.general: A mortal hero.
notes.here: He and Thetis are Achilles’s parents.

notes.label: Achilles
notes.general: The greatest Greek warrior in the Trojan War.
notes.here: His power in battle and courage are pictured through broken enemy ranks and a lion’s heart.

notes.label: Aeneas
notes.general: A Trojan hero, son of Aphrodite and Anchises.
notes.here: His birth follows his parents’ meeting on Mount Ida.

notes.label: Anchises
notes.general: A mortal man from the region of Troy.
notes.here: Aphrodite’s lover and Aeneas’s father.

notes.label: Mount Ida
notes.general: A mountain near Troy.
notes.here: Its “folds” are its many ridges and valleys.

notes.label: Circe
notes.general: A goddess skilled in magic who lives on an island.
notes.here: She has Agrius and Latinus with Odysseus.

notes.label: Helios
notes.general: The god of the Sun.
notes.here: Circe’s father and Hyperion’s son.

notes.label: Hyperion
notes.general: A Titan, one of the older generation of gods.
notes.here: Helios’s father and Circe’s grandfather.

notes.label: Odysseus
notes.general: A Greek hero famous for his cleverness and long journey home from Troy.
notes.here: He has children with both Circe and Calypso.

notes.label: Agrius
